1401.d: A chief of the tribe of Manasseh (Num. 34:23).

1404.d: The son and successor of Nahash, king of Moab. David’s messengers, sent on an embassy of condolence to him to Rabbah Ammon, his capital, were so grossly insulted that he proclaimed war against Hanun.

1407.d: Heb. haran; i.e., “mountaineer.” The eldest son of Terah, brother of Abraham and Nahor, and father of Lot, Milcah, and Iscah. He died before his father (Gen. 11:27), in Ur of the Chaldees.

1408.d: The son of Caleb of Judah (1 Chr. 2:46) by his concubine Ephah.

1410.d: (a Persian word meaning “ass-driver”), one of the seven eunuchs or chamberlains of king Ahasuerus (Esther 1:10; 7:9).

1413.d: Zeal of Jehovah, (Neh. 3:8) “of the goldsmiths,” one whose son helped to repair the wall of Jerusalem.

1416.d: The head of the second course of priests (1 Chr. 24:8).

1420.d: A chief of the tribe of Asher (1 Chr. 7:36).

1422.d: Worker or enchanter, one of the Nethinim (Ezra 2:52; Neh. 7:54).

1423.d: Elevated, (1 Chr. 4:8), a descendant of Judah.

1425.d: Eager, the father of Meshullemeth, the wife of king Manasseh (2 Kings 21:19) and mother of king Amon.

1426.d: Favoured by Jehovah, one of the sons of Pedaiah (1 Chr. 3:20), of the royal line of David.

1427.d: Bristling or hated, a Benjamite (1 Chr. 9:7).

1433.d: One of the chief Levites (2 Chr. 35:9).

1434.d: One of the chief priests in the time of Ezra (Ezra 8:24).

1440.d: One of the Levites whom Ezra appointed to interpret the law to the people (Neh. 9:5).

1441.d: Consideration in judging, stood at Ezra’s left hand when he read the law (Neh. 8:4).

1445.d: Ibid., a descendant of David (1 Chr. 3:20).

1447.d: Stood on Ezra’s left hand while he read the law (Neh. 8:4).

1414.d: Poverty, “keeper of the wardrobe,” i.e., of the sacerdotal vestments (2 Chr. 34:22); called Harhas 2 Kings 22:14. He was husband of the prophetess Huldah.

1450.d: A Levite of the family of Merari (Neh. 11:15; 1 Chr. 9:14).

1451.d: Uncovered, one of the Nethinim (Ezra 2:43; Neh. 7:46).

1452.d: Verity, one of the eunuchs or chamberlains in the palace of Ahasuerus (Esther 4:5, 6, 9, 10).

1455.d: Exploration, one of the temple porters or janitors (Ezra 2:42). He returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel.

1460.d: A priest who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:2).

1461.d: One of the sons of Cush (Gen. 10:7).

1463.d: Whom God beholds, an officer of Ben-hadad II., king of Syria, who ultimately came to the throne, according to the word of the Lord to Elijah (1 Kings 19:15), after he had put the king to death (2 Kings 8:15). His interview with Elisha is mentioned in 2 Kings 8.

1465.d: Court of death, the third son of Joktan, and a region in Arabia-Felix settled by him (Gen. 10:26; 1 Chr. 1:20). It is probably the modern province of Hadramaut, situated on the Indian Ocean east of the modern Yemen.

1468.d: Vision, one of the sons of Nahor (Gen. 22:22).

1469.d: Son of Beriah and grandson of Asher (Gen. 46:17; 1 Chr. 7:31, 32).

1470.d: The Kenite (Judg. 4:11, 17; 5:24), a descendant of Hobab. His wife Jael received Sisera (q.v.) into her tent and then killed him.

1472.d: One of the seven heads of the families of the Gadites (1 Chr. 5:13).

1475.d: The third son of Kohath the Levite (Ex. 6:18; 1 Chr. 6:2, 18).

1477.d: Eunuch, had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus (Esther 2:8).

1478.d: Rust, (1 Chr. 4:5, 7), one of the wives of Ashur.

1480.d: Fatness, one of David’s warriors (2 Sam. 23:29).

1479.d: Zech. 6:10, one who returned from Babylon.

1484.d: Elevation, father of Joseph in the line of our Lord’s ancestry (Luke 3:23).

1485.d: Smooth-tongued, one of the chief priests in the time of Joiakim (Neh. 12:15).

1486.d: Strong, father of Eliab, who was “captain of the children of Zebulun” (Num. 1:9; 2:7).

1488.d: 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chr. 2:6, a son of Zerah, noted for his wisdom.

1489.d: 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chr. 2:6, a son of Zerah, noted for his wisdom.

1490.d: Grandson of Samuel (1 Chr. 6:33; 15:17), to whom the 88th Psalm probably was inscribed. He was one of the “seers” named in 2 Chr. 29:14, 30, and took a leading part in the administration of the sacred services.

1493.d: Favour of Hadad, the name of a Levite after the Captivity (Ezra 3:9).

1497.d: The second son of Asher (1 Chr. 4:6).

1503.d: Mercury-born, at one time Paul’s fellow-labourer in Asia Minor, who, however, afterwards abandoned him, along with one Phygellus, probably on account of the perils by which they were beset (2 Tim. 1:15).

1505.d: Herod’s son by Malthace (Matt. 14:1; Luke 3:1, 19; 9:7; Acts 13:1).

1506.d: Son of Aristobulus and Bernice, and grandson of Herod the Great. He was made tetrarch of the provinces formerly held by Lysanias II., and ultimately possessed the entire kingdom of his grandfather, Herod the Great, with the title of king.
1506.e: Herod kills James, An angel rescues Peter from prison, Herod dies, Herod imprisons Peter

1507.d: (Matt. 14:3-11; Mark 6:17-28; Luke 3:19), the daughter of Aristobulus and Bernice. While residing at Rome with her husband Herod Philip I. and her daughter, Herod Antipas fell in with her during one of his journeys to that city.

1508.d: A Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes and calls his “kinsman” (Rom. 16:11).

1510.d: Dread, a descendant of Canaan, and the ancestor of the Hittites (Gen. 10:18; Deut. 7:1), who dwelt in the vicinity of Hebron (Gen. 23:3, 7). The Hittites were a Hamitic race. They are called “the sons of Heth” (Gen. 23:3, 5, 7, 10, 16, 18, 20).

1512.d: Son of Ahaz (2 Kings 18:1; 2 Chr. 29:1), whom he succeeded on the throne of the kingdom of Judah. He reigned twenty-nine years (B.C. 726-697). The history of this king is contained in 2 Kings 18:20, Isa. 36-39, and 2 Chr. 29-32.

1515.d: Vision, the father of Tabrimon, and grandfather of Ben-hadad, king of Syria (1 Kings 15:18).

1516.d: The head of the seventeenth course of the priests (1 Chr. 24:15).

1517.d: Neh. 10:20, one who sealed Nehemiah’s covenant.

1518.d: A Carmelite, one of David’s warriors (1 Chr. 11:37).

1519.d: One of the sons of Reuben (Gen. 46:9; Ex. 6:14).

1520.d: The older of the two sons of Pharez (Gen. 46:12).

1522.d: Life of (i.e., from) God, a native of Bethel, who built (i.e., fortified) Jericho some seven hundred years after its destruction by the Israelites. There fell on him for such an act the imprecation of Joshua (6:26).

1524.d: The high priest in the reign of Josiah (1 Chr. 6:13; Ezra 7:1). To him and his deputy (2 Kings 23:5), along with the ordinary priests and the Levites who had charge of the gates, was entrusted the purification of the temple in Jerusalem.

1530.d: Praising, a Pirathonite, father of the judge Abdon (Judg. 12:13, 15).

1532.d: Also “Huram” and “Horam,” king of Tyre. He entered into an alliance with David, and assisted him in building his palace by sending him able workmen, and also cedar-trees and fir-trees from Lebanon (2 Sam. 5:11; 1 Chr. 14:1).

1533.d: The “master workman” whom Hiram sent to Solomon. He was the son of a widow of Dan, and of a Tyrian father. In 2 Chr.

1534.d: One of the original tribes scattered over Palestine, from Hermon to Gibeon in the south. The name is interpreted as “midlanders” or “villagers” (Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15). They were probably a branch of the Hittites.

1537.d: Beloved, the Kenite, has been usually identified with Jethro (q.v.), Ex. 18:5, 27; comp. Num. 10:29, 30. In Judg. 4:11, the word rendered “father-in-law” means properly any male relative by marriage (comp. Gen.

1545.d: One of the Levites who assisted Ezra in expounding the law (Neh. 8:7; 9:5).

1547.d: Neh. 10:18, a Levite who sealed the covenant.

1548.d: Partridge, one of the daughters of Zelophehad the Gileadite, to whom portions were assigned by Moses (Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11).

1549.d: Jehovah impels, the king of Hebron who joined the league against Gibeon. He and his allies were defeated (Josh. 10:3, 5, 16-27).

1550.d: Pugilist or client, one of the two sons of Eli, the high priest (1 Sam. 1:3; 2:34), who, because he was “very old,” resigned to them the active duties of his office.

1554.d: A Levite of the family of Merari (1 Chr. 16:38).

1555.d: Salvation, the son of Beeri, and author of the book of prophecies bearing his name. He belonged to the kingdom of Israel. “His Israelitish origin is attested by the peculiar, rough, Aramaizing diction, pointing to the northern part of Palestine

1559.d: The last king of Israel. He conspired against and slew his predecessor, Pekah (Isa. 7:16), but did not ascend the throne till after an interregnum of warfare of eight years (2 Kings 17:1, 2).

1560.d: 1 Chr. 27:20. The ruler of Ephraim in David’s time.

1562.d: A stroke, great-grandson of Asher (1 Chr. 7:35).

1566.d: Circle, the second son of Aram (Gen. 10:23), and grandson of Shem.

1567.d: Weasel, a prophetess; the wife of Shallum. She was consulted regarding the “book of the law” discovered by the high priest Hilkiah (2 Kings 22:14-20; 2 Chr. 34:22-28).

1571.d: The husband of Miriam, Moses’ sister (Ex. 17:10-12). He was associated with Aaron in charge of the people when Moses was absent on Sinai (Ex. 24:14). He was probably of the tribe of Judah, and grandfather of Bezaleel (Ex. 31:2; 35:30; 1 Chr. 2:19).

1572.d: One of the five princes of Midian who were defeated and slain by the Israelites under the command of Phinehas (Num. 31:8).

1521.d: Linen-worker, one of David’s heroes, a native of the valley of Mount Gaash (1 Chr. 11:32).

1569.d: Generally “Huram,” one of the sons of Bela (1 Chr. 8:5).

1584.d: Chosen, one of David’s sons (1 Chr. 3:6; 2 Sam. 5:15).

1588.d: Illustrious, the tenth judge of Israel (Judg. 12:8-10). He ruled seven years.

1591.d: Timely. The father of Ahinadab, who was one of Solomon’s purveyors (1 Kings 4:14).

1593.d: Lovely. The son of Zechariah (1 Chr. 27:21), the ruler of Manasseh in David’s time.

1594.d: Lovely. A prophet of Judah who wrote the history of Rehoboam and Abijah (2 Chr. 12:15). He has been identified with Oded (2 Chr. 15:1).

1598.d: Num. 13:7, one of the spies of the tribe of Issachar.

1599.d: Son of Nathan of Zobah, and one of David’s warriors (2 Sam. 23:36).

2982.d: An Ahohite, one of David’s chief warriors (1 Chr. 11:29); called also Zalmon (2 Sam. 23:28).

597.d: Replenisher, the father of Micaiah the prophet (2 Chr. 18:7, 8).

599.d: The head of the sixteenth priestly order (1 Chr. 24:14).

606.d: Set free by Jehovah, a chief of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:25).

608.d: A Jairite and priest, a royal chaplain (2 Sam. 20:26) or confidential adviser (comp. 2 Sam. 8:18; 1 Chr. 18:17).

609.d: A Tekoite, one of David’s thirty warriors (2 Sam. 23:26).

610.d: An Ithrite, also one of David’s heroes (2 Sam. 23:38).

611.d: Runner; wild ass, one of the antediluvian patriarchs, the father of Mehujael (Gen. 4:18), and grandson of Cain.

612.d: Citizen, chief of an Edomite tribe in Mount Seir (Gen. 36:43).

616.d: The only son of Abraham by Sarah. He was the longest lived of the three patriarchs (Gen. 21:1-3). He was circumcised when eight days old (4-7); and when he was probably two years old a great feast was held in connection with his being weaned.

617.d: The son of Amoz (Isa. 1:1; 2:1), who was apparently a man of humble rank. His wife was called “the prophetess” (8:3), either because she was endowed with the prophetic gift, like Deborah (Judg.

618.d: Spy, the daughter of Haran and sister of Milcah and Lot (Gen. 11:29, 31).

620.d: Leaving, one of Abraham’s sons by Keturah (Gen. 25:2).

621.d: My seat at Nob, one of the Rephaim, whose spear was three hundred shekels in weight. He was slain by Abishai (2 Sam. 21:16, 17).

630.d: Abraham’s eldest son, by Hagar the concubine (Gen. 16:15; 17:23). He was born at Mamre, when Abraham was eighty-six years of age, eleven years after his arrival in Canaan (16:3; 21:5). At the age of thirteen he was circumcised (17:25).

631.d: The son of Nethaniah, “of the seed royal” (Jer. 40:8, 15). He plotted against Gedaliah, and treacherously put him and others to death. He carried off many captives, “and departed to go over to the Ammonites.”

636.d: Son of Obadiah, and viceroy of Zebulun under David and Solomon (1 Chr. 27:19).

643.d: A Gibeonite who joined David at Ziklag, “a hero among the thirty and over the thirty” (1 Chr. 12:4).

682.d: One who follows on another’s heels; supplanter, (Gen. 25:26; 27:36; Hos. 12:2-4), the second born of the twin sons of Isaac by Rebekah. He was born probably at Lahai-roi, when his father was fifty-nine and Abraham one hundred and fifty-nine years old.

645.d: Hired (Gen. 30:18). “God hath given me,” said Leah, “my hire (Heb. sekhari)...and she called his name Issachar.” He was Jacob’s ninth son, and was born in Padan-aram (comp. 28:2). He had four sons at the going down into Egypt (46:13; Num. 26:23, 25).

649.d: Palm isle, the fourth and youngest son of Aaron (1 Chr. 6:3). He was consecrated to the priesthood along with his brothers (Ex. 6:23); and after the death of Nadab and Abihu, he and Eleazar alone discharged the functions of that office (Lev. 10:6, 12; Num.

656.d: A native of Gath, a Philistine, who had apparently the command of the six hundred heroes who formed David’s band during his wanderings (2 Sam. 15:19-22; comp. 1 Sam. 23:13; 27:2; 30:9, 10).

657.d: A Benjamite, one of David’s thirty heroes (2 Sam. 23:29).

658.d: Oil, one of the sons of Kohath, and grandson of Levi (Ex. 6:18, 21; Num. 16:1).

660.d: Heel-catcher, a form of the name Jacob, one of the descendants of Simeon (1 Chr. 4:36).

661.d: A wild she-goat, one of the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from the Captivity (Neh. 7:58).

662.d: Concealer, the second of Esau’s three sons by Aholibamah (Gen. 36:5, 14).

663.d: Mourner, one of the chief Gadites (1 Chr. 5:12).

666.d: Made by God, one of David’s body-guard, the son of Abner (1 Chr. 27:21), called Jasiel in 1 Chr. 11:47.

668.d: The son of Jeremiah, and one of the chief Rechabites (Jer. 35:3).

671.d: Comforted by Jehovah, a descendant of Merari the Levite (1 Chr. 24:26, 27).

672.d: Comforted by God, a Levitical musician (1 Chr. 15:18).

673.d: A stream, a descendant of Cain, and brother of Jubal; “the father of such as dwell in tents and have cattle” (Gen. 4:20). This description indicates that he led a wandering life.

674.d: The father of Shallum (2 Kings 15:10, 13, 14), who usurped the throne of Israel on the death of Zachariah.

675.d: A descendant of Judah, of whom it is recorded that “God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chr. 4:9, 10).

676.d: A king of Hazor, at the time of the entrance of Israel into Canaan (Josh. 11:1-14), whose overthrow and that of the northern chief with whom he had entered into a confederacy against Joshua was the crowning act in the conquest of the land (11:21-23; comp.

677.d: Another king of Hazor, called “the king of Canaan,” who overpowered the Israelites of the north one hundred and sixty years after Joshua’s death, and for twenty years held them in painful subjection.

678.d: Mourner, one of the chief Gadite “brothers” in Bashan (1 Chr. 5:13).

679.d: The fourth son of Simeon (Gen. 46:10), called also Jarib (1 Chr. 4:24).

680.d: One of the priests who returned from the Exile (1 Chr. 9:10).

681.d: The head of one of the courses (the twenty-first) of priests (1 Chr. 24:17).

686.d: One of the chiefs who subscribed the covenant (Neh. 10:21).

687.d: The last high priest mentioned in the Old Testament (Neh. 12:11, 22), sons of Jonathan.

688.d: Judge, a Meronothite who assisted in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem (Neh. 3:7).

692.d: A son of Shimei, and grandson of Gershom (1 Chr. 23:10).

693.d: One of the sons of Shelomoth, of the family of Kohath (1 Chr. 24:22).

694.d: A Levite of the family of Merari, one of the overseers of the repairs of the temple under Josiah (2 Chr. 34:12).

697.d: A priest who accompanied the removal of the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 16:6).

698.d: The third son of Hebron (1 Chr. 23:19).

699.d: The son of Zechariah, a Levite of the family of Asaph (2 Chr. 20:14-17). He encouraged Jehoshaphat against the Moabites and Ammonites.

701.d: Grasper, a descendant of Caleb, of the family of Hezron (1 Chr. 2:47).

706.d: Allotted by God, the first of the sons of Naphtali (Gen. 46:24).

707.d: Returner, the son of Meshullam, and father of Adiel (1 Chr. 9:12).

664.d: The father of Elhanan, who slew Lahmi, the brother of Goliath (1 Chr. 20:5).

710.d: A Benjamite, the father of Mordecai, Esther’s uncle (Esther 2:5).

711.d: A ruler of the synagogue at Capernaum, whose only daughter Jesus restored to life (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41).

712.d: Pious, the father of Agur (Prov. 30:1). Nothing is known of him.

714.d: Chief of the twelfth priestly order (1 Chr. 24:12).

715.d: Lodger, the last of the four sons of Ezra, of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr. 4:17).

716.d: One of those who opposed Moses in Egypt (2 Tim. 3:8).

737.d: Upright. “The Book of Jasher,” rendered in the LXX.

1638.d: The third of Issachar’s four sons (1 Chr. 7:1); called also Job (Gen. 46:13).

752.d: A priest in Jerusalem after the Exile (1 Chr. 9:10).

753.d: Knowing Jehovah. The chief of one of the courses of the priests (1 Chr. 24:7).

754.d: One of those who repaired the walls of Jerusalem after the return from Babylon (Neh. 3:10).

757.d: One of the sons of Benjamin, whose descendants numbered 17,200 warriors (1 Chr. 7:6, 10, 11).

758.d: A Shimrite, one of David’s bodyguard (1 Chr. 11:45). Probably same as in 12:20.

760.d: A Korhite of the family of Ebiasaph, and one of the gate-keepers to the temple (1 Chr. 26:2).

765.d: A Levite of the family of Merari (2 Chr. 29:12).

766.d: One of the Levitical attendants at the temple, a descendant of Shubael (1 Chr. 24:20).

767.d: A Meronothite, herdsman of the asses under David and Solomon (1 Chr. 27:30).

770.d: One of the Levites “of the second degree,” appointed to conduct the music on the occasion of the ark’s being removed to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 15:18, 20).

772.d: A Hachmonite, a tutor in the family of David toward the close of his reign (1 Chr. 27:32).

773.d: The second of Jehoshaphat’s six sons (2 Chr. 21:2).

774.d: One of the Levites of the family of Heman who assisted Hezekiah in his work of reformation (2 Chr. 29:14).

781.d: Jehovah strengthens, one of the chiefs of Ephraim (2 Chr. 28:12).

783.d: Jehovah his ornament, the wife of King Jehoash, and mother of King Amaziah (2 Kings 14:2).

784.d: The son and successor of Jehu, king of Israel (2 Kings 10:35). He reigned seventeen years, and followed the evil ways of the house of Jeroboam.

785.d: A Korhite, the head of one of the divisions of the temple porters (1 Chr. 26:3).

791.d: Succeeded his father Jehoiakin (B.C. 599) when only eight years of age, and reigned for one hundred days (2 Chr. 36:9). He is also called Jeconiah (Jer. 24:1; 27:20, etc.), and Coniah (22:24; 37:1). He was succeeded by his uncle, Mattaniah = Zedekiah (q.v.).

792.d: The father of Benaiah, who was one of David’s chief warriors (2 Sam. 8:18; 20:23).

793.d: The high priest at the time of Athaliah’s usurpation of the throne of Judah. He married Jehosheba, or Jehoshabeath, the daughter of king Jehoram (2 Chr.

1085.d: He whom Jehovah has set up, the second son of Josiah, and eighteenth king of Judah, which he ruled over for eleven years (B.C. 610-599). His original name was Eliakim (q.v.). On the death of his father his younger brother Jehoahaz (=Shallum, Jer.

800.d: One of the stewards of David’s store-houses (1 Chr. 27:25).

801.d: A Levite who taught the law to the people of Judah (2 Chr. 17:8).

803.d: The eldest son and successor of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He reigned eight years (B.C. 892-885) alone as king of Judah, having been previously for some years associated with his father (2 Chr. 21:5, 20; 2 Kings 8:16).

805.d: A priest sent by Jehoshaphat to instructruct the people in Judah (2 Chr. 17:8).

811.d: Jehovah-swearing, the daughter of Jehoram, the king of Israel. She is called Jehoshabeath in 2 Chr. 22:11. She was the only princess of the royal house who was married to a high priest, Jehoiada (2 Chr. 22:11).

806.d: Son of Ahilud, “recorder” or annalist under David and Solomon (2 Sam. 8:16), a state officer of high rank, chancellor or vizier of the kingdom.

808.d: The son and successor of Asa, king of Judah. After fortifying his kingdom against Israel (2 Chr. 17:1, 2), he set himself to cleanse the land of idolatry (1 Kings 22:43).

809.d: The son of Nimshi, and father of Jehu, king of Israel (2 Kings 9:2, 14).

810.d: One of the priests who accompanied the removal of the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 15:24).

812.d: The son of Shomer, one of the two conspirators who put king Jehoash to death in Millo in Jerusalem (2 Kings 12:21).

813.d: The son of Obed-edom (1 Chr. 26:4), one of the Levite porters.

816.d: The son of Hanani, a prophet of Judah (1 Kings 16:1, 7; 2 Chr. 19:2; 20:34), who pronounced the sentence of God against Baasha, the king of Israel.

817.d: King of Israel, the son of Jehoshaphat (2 Kings 9:2), and grandson of Nimshi. The story of his exaltation to the throne is deeply interesting.

818.d: The son of Obed, and father of Azariah (1 Chr. 2:38).

820.d: One of the Benjamite slingers that joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:3).

823.d: A Jew, son of Nethaniah. He was sent by the princes to invite Baruch to read Jeremiah’s roll to them (Jer. 36:14, 21).

827.d: One of the Levites who took part in praising God on the removal of the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 16:5).

830.d: 2 Chr. 29:13. A Levite of the sons of Asaph.

831.d: One of the chief Levites, who made an offering for the restoration of the Passover by Josiah (2 Chr. 35:9).

837.d: Dove, the eldest of Job’s three daughters born after his time of trial (Job 42:14).

838.d: One of Simeon’s five sons (1 Chr. 4:24), called also Jemuel (Gen. 46:10).

839.d: Whom God sets free, or the breaker through, a “mighty man of valour” who delivered Israel from the oppression of the Ammonites (Judg. 11:1-33), and judged Israel six years (12:7).

840.d: The father of Caleb, who was Joshua’s companion in exploring Canaan (Num. 13:6), a Kenezite (Josh. 14:14).

841.d: One of the descendants of Asher (1 Chr. 7:38).

843.d: The son of Hezron, the brother of Caleb (1 Chr. 2:9, 25, 26, etc.).

844.d: The son of Kish, a Levite (1 Chr. 24:29).

846.d: A son of Ezra probably (1 Chr. 4:18).

848.d: The father of Hamutal (2 Kings 23:31), the wife of Josiah.

849.d: One of the chiefs of the tribe of Manasseh on the east of Jordan (1 Chr. 5:24).

850.d: A Benjamite slinger who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:4).

851.d: A Gadite who joined David in the wilderness (1 Chr. 12:10).

853.d: One of the “greater prophets” of the Old Testament, son of Hilkiah (q.v.), a priest of Anathoth (Jer. 1:1; 32:6). He was called to the prophetical office when still young (1:6), in the thirteenth year of Josiah (B.C. 628).

864.d: One of the sons of Bela (1 Chr. 7:7).

866.d: A Benjamite slinger who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:5).

867.d: A Levitical musician under Heman his father (1 Chr. 25:4).

870.d: A Levite, one of the overseers of the temple offerings (2 Chr. 31:13) in the reign of Hezekiah.

872.d: The son of Nebat (1 Kings 11:26-39), “an Ephrathite,” the first king of the ten tribes, over whom he reigned twenty-two years (B.C. 976-945).

873.d: Jeroboam II., the son and successor of Jehoash, and the fourteenth king of Israel, over which he ruled for forty-one years, B.C. 825-784 (2 Kings 14:23).

874.d: Father of Elkanah, and grandfather of the prophet Samuel (1 Sam. 1:1).

877.d: 1 Chr. 9:12; a priest, perhaps the same as in Neh. 11:12.

879.d: The father of Azareel, the “captain” of the tribe of Dan (1 Chr. 27:22).

880.d: 2 Chr. 23:1; one whose son assisted in placing Joash on the throne.

881.d: Contender with the shame; i.e., idol, a surname also of Gideon (2 Sam. 11:21).

882.d: Possession, or possessed; i.e., “by a husband”, the wife of Uzziah, and mother of king Jotham (2 Kings 15:33).

883.d: One of the three sons of Hananiah (1 Chr. 3:21).

647.d: A Kohathite Levite, the father of Joram, of the family of Eliezer (1 Chr. 26:25); called also Isshiah (24:21).

885.d: One of the sons of Jeduthum (1 Chr. 25:3, 15).

334.d: Upright towards God, the head of the seventh division of Levitical musicians (1 Chr. 25:14).

888.d: Seat of his father, the head of the fourteenth division of priests (1 Chr. 24:13).

889.d: Uprightness, the first of the three sons of Caleb by Azubah (1 Chr. 2:18).

892.d: A Levite appointed by Hezekiah to distribute offerings in the priestly cities (2 Chr. 31:15).

899.d: Head of the ninth priestly order (Ezra 2:36); called also Jeshuah (1 Chr. 24:11).

903.d: Firm, or a gift, a son of Obed, the son of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:17, 22; Matt. 1:5, 6; Luke 3:32). He was the father of eight sons, the youngest of whom was David (1 Sam. 17:12). The phrase “stem of Jesse” is used for the family of David (Isa.

905.d: Anointed, the Greek translation of the Hebrew word rendered “Messiah” (q.v.), the official title of our Lord, occurring five hundred and fourteen times in the New Testament.
905.e: Jesus ascends to Heaven, The Holy Spirit is promised, God creates all things

906.d: The oldest of Gideon’s seventy sons (Judg. 8:20).

907.d: The father of Amasa, David’s general (1 Kings 2:5, 32); called Ithra (2 Sam. 17:25).

910.d: A peg, or a prince, one of the Edomitish kings of Mount Seir (Gen. 36:40).

2431.d: “The priest of Midian,” Moses’ father-in-law (Ex. 2:18)=Raguel (Num. 10:29). If he be identified with Jethro (q.v.), then this may be regarded as his proper name, and Jether or Jethro (i.e., “excellency”) as his official title.

911.d: An enclosure, one of the twelve sons of Ishmael (Gen. 25:15).

912.d: Snatched away by God, a descendant of Zerah (1 Chr. 9:6).

913.d: The oldest of Esau’s three sons by Aholibamah (Gen. 36:5, 14, 18).

1601.d: A son of Bilhan, grandson of Benjamin (1 Chr. 7:10).

1602.d: A Levite, one of the sons of Shimei (1 Chr. 23:10, 11).

1603.d: One of the three sons of Rehoboam (2 Chr. 11:19).

667.d: A Maachathite (2 Kings 25:23; Jer. 40:8; 42:1). He is also called Azariah (Jer. 43:2).

1605.d: Chaste, the daughter of Ethbaal, the king of the Zidonians, and the wife of Ahab, the king of Israel (1 Kings 16:31). This was the “first time that a king of Israel had allied himself by marriage with a heathen princess

1608.d: Assembled by God, a son of Azmaveth. He was one of the Benjamite archers who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:3).

1617.d: One of the three sons of Zeruiah, David’s sister, and “captain of the host” during the whole of David’s reign (2 Sam. 2:13; 10:7; 11:1; 1 Kings 11:15). His father’s name is nowhere mentioned, although his sepulchre at Bethlehem is mentioned (2 Sam. 2:32).

1621.d: The son of Asaph, and “recorder” (q.v.) or chronicler to King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:18, 26, 37).

1623.d: One of the sons of Obed-edom (1 Chr. 26:4), a Korhite porter.

1626.d: Son of Joahaz, and “recorder” (q.v.) or keeper of the state archives under King Josiah (2 Chr. 34:8).

1627.d: (2 Chr. 34:8), a contracted form of Jehoahaz (q.v.).

1628.d: The grandson of Zerubbabel, in the lineage of Christ (Luke 3:27); the same as Hananiah (1 Chr. 3:19).

1629.d: The wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee (Luke 8:3). She was one of the women who ministered to our Lord, and to whom he appeared after his resurrection (Luke 8:3; 24:10).

1630.d: A contracted form of Jehoash, the father of Gideon (Judg. 6:11, 29; 8:13, 29, 32).

1631.d: One of King Ahab’s sons (1 Kings 22:26).

1633.d: The son and successor of Jehoahaz, king of Israel (2 Kings 14:1; comp. 12:1; 13:10). When he ascended the throne the kingdom was suffering from the invasion of the Syrians.

1636.d: One of the Benjamite archers who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:3).

1637.d: One who had charge of the royal stores of oil under David and Solomon (1 Chr. 27:28).

1639.d: Persecuted, an Arabian patriarch who resided in the land of Uz (q.v.). While living in the midst of great prosperity, he was suddenly overwhelmed by a series of sore trials that fell upon him. Amid all his sufferings he maintained his integrity.

1640.d: One of the sons of Joktan, and founder of an Arabian tribe (Gen. 10:29).

1642.d: A Canaanitish king (Josh. 11:1) who joined the confederacy against Joshua.

1645.d: Jehovah is her glory, the wife of Amram, and the mother of Miriam, Aaron, and Moses (Num. 26:59). She is spoken of as the sister of Kohath, Amram’s father (Ex. 6:20; comp. 16, 18; 2:1-10).

1647.d: The oldest of Samuel’s two sons appointed by him as judges in Beersheba (1 Sam. 8:2).

1653.d: One of David’s famous warriors (1 Chr. 11:38).

1654.d: A Levite of the family of Gershom (1 Chr. 15:7, 11).

1660.d: The second of the twelve minor prophets. He was the son of Pethuel. His personal history is only known from his book.

1661.d: A Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:7).

1662.d: Jehovah is his help, one of the Korhites who became part of David’s body-guard (1 Chr. 12:6).

1666.d: Son of Careah, one of the Jewish chiefs who rallied round Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made governor in Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:23; Jer. 40:8). He warned Gedaliah of the plans of Ishmael against him, a warning which was unheeded (Jer. 40:13, 16).

1667.d: The oldest of King Josiah’s sons (1 Chr. 3:15).

1671.d: One of the Gadite heroes who joined David in the desert of Judah (1 Chr. 12:12).

1676.d: The “forerunner of our Lord.” We have but fragmentary and imperfect accounts of him in the Gospels. He was of priestly descent. His father, Zacharias, was a priest of the course of Abia (1 Chr.

1677.d: THE APOSTLE, brother of James the “Greater” (Matt. 4:21; 10:2; Mark 1:19; 3:17; 10:35). He was one, probably the younger, of the sons of Zebedee (Matt. 4:21) and Salome (Matt. 27:56; comp. Mark 15:40), and was born at Bethsaida.

1678.d: One who, with Annas and Caiaphas, sat in judgment on the apostles Peter and John (Acts 4:6). He was of the kindred of the high priest; otherwise unknown.

1681.d: (whom Jehovah has set up) = Jehoiakim, a high priest, the son and successor of Jeshua (Neh. 12:10, 12, 26).

797.d: The founder of one of the courses of the priests (Neh. 11:10).

1682.d: Ezra 8:16, a “man of understanding” whom Ezra sent to “bring ministers for the house of God.”

1684.d: Whom Jehovah has set up, one of the descendants of Shelah (1 Chr. 4:22).

1685.d: Snarer, the second son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen. 25:2, 3; 1 Chr. 1:32).

799.d: A son of Rechab, the founder of a tribe who bound themselves by a vow to abstain from wine (Jer. 35:6-19). There were different settlements of Rechabites (Judg. 1:16; 4:11; 1 Chr. 2:55). His interview and alliance with Jehu are mentioned in 2 Kings 10:15-23.

1688.d: Son of Shammah, and David’s nephew, and also one of his chief warriors (2 Sam. 21:21). He slew a giant in Gath.

1689.d: A dove, the son of Amittai of Gath-hepher. He was a prophet of Israel, and predicted the restoration of the ancient boundaries (2 Kings 14:25-27) of the kingdom.

1687.d: The father of the apostles Peter (John 21:15-17) and Andrew; but the reading should be (also in 1:42), as in the Revised Version, “John,” instead of Jonas.

1691.d: A Levite descended from Gershom (Judg. 18:30). His history is recorded in 17:7-13 and 18:30.

1692.d: The eldest son of king Saul, and the bosom friend of David. He is first mentioned when he was about thirty years of age, some time after his father’s accession to the throne (1 Sam. 13:2). Like his father, he was a man of great strength and activity (2 Sam.

1693.d: Son of the high priest Abiathar, and one who adhered to David at the time of Absalom’s rebellion (2 Sam. 15:27, 36). He is the last descendant of Eli of whom there is any record.

1705.d: The son of Tou, king of Hamath, sent by his father to congratulate David on his victory over Hadarezer, king of Syria (1 Chr. 18:10; called Joram 2 Sam. 8:10).

1708.d: One of the Benjamite archers who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:4).

1710.d: The elder of the two sons of Jacob by Rachel (Gen. 30:23, 24), who, on the occasion of his birth, said, “God hath taken away [Heb. ‘asaph] my reproach.” “The Lord shall add [Heb. yoseph] to me another son” (Gen. 30:24).

1712.d: One of the sons of Asaph, head of the first division of sacred musicians (1 Chr. 25:2, 9).

1715.d: The foster-father of our Lord (Matt. 1:16; Luke 3:23). He lived at Nazareth in Galilee (Luke 2:4). He is called a “just man.” He was by trade a carpenter (Matt. 13:55).

1716.d: A native of Arimathea, probably the Ramah of the Old Testament (1 Sam. 1:19), a man of wealth, and a member of the Sanhedrim (Matt. 27:57

1718.d: The son of Judah, and father of Semei (Luke 3:26). Other two of the same name in the ancestry of Christ are also mentioned (3:24, 30).

1734.d: The youngest of Gideon’s seventy sons. He escaped when the rest were put to death by the order of Abimelech (Judg. 9:5).

1735.d: The son and successor of Uzziah on the throne of Judah.

1750.d: The father of Simeon in Christ’s maternal ancestry (Luke 3:30).

1770.d: Eastward, the last-named of the sons of Ishmael (Gen. 25:15).

1772.d: Dwarf, a Levite who assisted Ezra in expounding the law to the people (Neh. 8:7; 10:10).

1774.d: Son of Shiphtan, appointed on behalf of the tribe of Ephraim to partition the land of Canaan (Num. 34:24).

1778.d: Caleb’s younger brother, and father of Othniel (Josh. 15:17), whose family was of importance in Israel down to the time of David (1 Chr. 27:15). Some think that Othniel (Judg. 1:13), and not Kenaz, was Caleb’s brother.

1780.d: Horn of the face-paint = cosmetic-box, the name of Job’s third daughter (Job. 42:14), born after prosperity had returned to him.

1782.d: Incense, the wife of Abraham, whom he married probably after Sarah’s death (Gen. 25:1-6), by whom he had six sons, whom he sent away into the east country. Her nationality is unknown. She is styled “Abraham’s concubine” (1 Chr. 1:32).

1784.d: A Benjamite, the son of Abiel, and father of king Saul (1 Sam. 9:1, 3; 10:11, 21; 14:51; 2 Sam. 21:14). All that is recorded of him is that he sent his son Saul in search of his asses that had strayed, and that he was buried in Zelah.

1785.d: A Levite of the family of Merari (1 Chr. 23:21; 24:29).

1786.d: A Levite in the time of Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29:12).

1790.d: Assembly, the second son of Levi, and father of Amram (Gen. 46:11). He came down to Egypt with Jacob, and lived to the age of one hundred and thirty-three years (Ex. 6:18).

1793.d: The third son of Esau, by Aholibamah (Gen. 36:14; 1 Chr. 1:35).

1795.d: A Levite, the son of Izhar, the brother of Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron (Ex. 6:21). The institution of the Aaronic priesthood and the Levitical service at Sinai was a great religious revolution. The old priesthood of the heads of families passed away.

1797.d: A Levite and temple-warder of the Korahites, the son of Asaph. He was father of Shallum and Meshelemiah, temple-porters (1 Chr. 9:19; 26:1).

1798.d: A Levitical porter at the east gate of the temple (2 Chr. 31:14).

1823.d: White, one of the two sons of Gershon, the son of Levi (Ex. 6:17; Num. 3:18, 21).

1803.d: The son of Bethuel, who was the son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. He lived at Haran in Mesopotamia. His sister Rebekah was Isaac’s wife (Gen. 24). Jacob, one of the sons of this marriage, fled to the house of Laban, whose daughters Leah and Rachel (ch.

1808.d: The fifth in descent from Cain. He was the first to violate the primeval ordinance of marriage (Gen. 4:18-24). His address to his two wives, Adah and Zillah (4:23, 24), is the only extant example of antediluvian poetry.

1809.d: The seventh in descent from Seth, being the only son of Methuselah. Noah was the oldest of his several sons (Gen. 5:25-31; Luke 3:36).

1810.d: Torches. Deborah is called “the wife of Lapidoth” (Judg. 4:4). Some have rendered the expression “a woman of a fiery spirit,” under the supposition that Lapidoth is not a proper name, a woman of a torch-like spirit.

1812.d: The brother of Mary and Martha of Bethany. He was raised from the dead after he had lain four days in the tomb (John 11:1-44). This miracle so excited the wrath of the Jews that they sought to put both Jesus and Lazarus to death.

1813.d: Weary, the eldest daughter of Laban, and sister of Rachel (Gen. 29:16). Jacob took her to wife through a deceit of her father (Gen. 29:23). She was “tender-eyed” (17). She bore to Jacob six sons (32-35), also one daughter, Dinah (30:21).

1815.d: Breast, the name of one of the apostles (Mark 3:18), called “Lebbaeus” in Matt.

1817.d: Dedicated to God, a king whom his mother instructed (Prov. 31:1-9). Nothing is certainly known concerning him. The rabbis identified him with Solomon.

1819.d: Peoples; nations, the last mentioned of the three sons of Dedan, and head of an Arabian tribe (Gen. 25:3).

1820.d: The third son of Jacob by Leah. The origin of the name is found in Leah’s words (Gen. 29:34), “This time will my husband be joined [Heb. yillaveh] unto me.” He is mentioned as taking a prominent part in avenging his sister Dinah (Gen. 34:25-31).

1822.d: The father of Matthat, and son of Simeon, of the ancestors of Christ (Luke 3:29).

1827.d: Not my people, a symbolical name given by God’s command to Hosea’s second son in token of Jehovah’s rejection of his people (Hos. 1:9, 10), his treatment of them as a foreign people. This Hebrew word is rendered by “not my people” in ver. 10; 2:23.

1829.d: Not pitied, the name of the prophet Hosea’s first daughter, a type of Jehovah’s temporary rejection of his people (Hos. 1:6; 2:23).

1828.d: The maternal grandmother of Timothy. She is commended by Paul for her faith (2 Tim. 1:5).

1830.d: (Heb. goral, a “pebble”), a small stone used in casting lots (Num. 33:54; Jonah 1:7). The lot was always resorted to by the Hebrews with strictest reference to the interposition of God, and as a method of ascertaining the divine will (Prov.
1830.e: Abraham is called to Canaan, Abraham and Lot Separate

1831.d: Coverer, one of the sons of Seir, the Horite (Gen. 36:20, 29).

1832.d: Brilliant star, a title given to the king of Babylon (Isa. 14:12) to denote his glory.

1833.d: Of Cyrene, a Christian teacher at Antioch (Acts 13:1), and Paul’s kinsman (Rom. 16:21). His name is Latin, but his birthplace seems to indicate that he was one of the Jews of Cyrene, in North Africa.

1834.d: The fourth son of Shem (Gen. 10:22; 1 Chr. 1:17), ancestor of the Lydians probably.

1835.d: Probably the same as Lud (2) (comp. Gen. 10:13; 1 Chr. 1:11). They are associated (Jer. 46:9) with African nations as mercenaries of the king of Egypt.

1836.d: The evangelist, was a Gentile. The date and circumstances of his conversion are unknown.
1836.e: Mission to Macedonia and Greece, Eutychus revived, Voyage to Miletus, Paul speaks to Ephesian Elders, Voyage from Miletus to Jerusalem, Paul visits elders in Je

1837.d: A woman of Thyatira, a “seller of purple,” who dwelt in Philippi (Acts 16:14, 15). She was not a Jewess but a proselyte. The Lord opened her heart as she heard the gospel from the lips of Paul (16:13).
1837.e: Lydia's Conversion, Paul and Silas released

1838.d: Tetrarch of Abilene (Luke 3:1), on the eastern slope of Anti-Lebanon, near the city of Damascus.

1839.d: A daughter of Talmai, king of the old native population of Geshur. She became one of David’s wives, and was the mother of Absalom (2 Sam. 3:3).

1841.d: The daughter of Abishalom (called Absalom, 2 Chr. 11:20-22), the third wife of Rehoboam, and mother of Abijam (1 Kings 15:2). She is called “Michaiah the daughter of Uriel,” who was the husband of Absalom’s daughter Tamar (2 Chr. 13:2).

1845.d: The father of Hanan, who was one of David’s body-guard (1 Chr. 11:43).

1934.d: The father of Achish, the king of Gath (1 Kings 2:39), called also Maoch (1 Sam. 27:2).

1849.d: One of the Levites whom David appointed as porter for the ark (1 Chr. 15:18, 20).

1850.d: One of the “captains of hundreds” associated with Jehoiada in restoring king Jehoash to the throne (2 Chr. 23:1).

1853.d: One who was sent by king Josiah to repair the temple (2 Chr. 34:8). He was governor (Heb. sar, rendered elsewhere in the Authorized Version “prince,” “chief captain,” chief ruler”) of Jerusalem.

1866.d: The father of the priest Zephaniah (Jer. 21:1; 37:3).

1870.d: Work of Jehovah, one of the priests resident at Jerusalem at the Captivity (1 Chr. 9:12).

1871.d: Small, a person named in our Lord’s ancestry (Luke 3:26).

1873.d: The head of the twenty-fourth priestly course (1 Chr. 24:18) in David’s reign.

1877.d: Manasseh’s oldest son (Josh. 17:1), or probably his only son (see 1 Chr. 7:14, 15; comp. Num. 26:29-33; Josh. 13:31). His descendants are referred to under the name of Machirites, being the offspring of Gilead (Num. 26:29).

1878.d: A descendant of the preceding, residing at Lo-debar, where he maintained Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth till he was taken under the care of David (2 Sam. 9:4), and where he afterwards gave shelter to David himself when he was a fugitive (17:27).

1880.d: Middle land, the third “son” of Japheth (Gen. 10:2), the name by which the Medes are known on the Assyrian monuments.

1882.d: Region of Gog, the second of the “sons” of Japheth (Gen. 10:2; 1 Chr. 1:5). In Ezekiel (38:2; 39:6) it is the name of a nation, probably some Scythian or Tartar tribe descended from Japheth.

1885.d: The son of Cainan, of the line of Seth (Gen. 5:12-17); called Maleleel (Luke 3:37).

1888.d: The daughter of Jerimoth, who was one of David’s sons. She was one of Rehoboam’s wives (2 Chr. 11:18).

150.d: A Kohathite Levite, father of Elkanah (1 Chr. 6:35).

1891.d: Another Kohathite Levite, of the time of Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29:12).

1893.d: Visions, a Kohathite Levite, chief of the twenty-third course of musicians (1 Chr. 25:4, 30).

1894.d: Plunder speedeth; spoil hasteth, (Isa. 8:1-3; comp. Zeph. 1:14), a name Isaiah was commanded first to write in large characters on a tablet, and afterwards to give as a symbolical name to a son that was to be born to him (Isa.

1895.d: Disease, one of the five daughters of Zelophehad (Num. 27:1-11) who had their father’s inheritance, the law of inheritance having been altered in their favour.

1897.d: Sickly, the elder of Elimelech the Bethlehemite’s two sons by Naomi. He married Ruth and died childless (Ruth 1:2, 5; 4:9, 10), in the land of Moab.

1898.d: Dance, the father of four sons (1 Kings 4:31) who were inferior in wisdom only to Solomon.

1899.d: Messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon (Mal. 4:4, 5, 6). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies.

1900.d: (2 Sam. 12:30, Heb., R.V., “their king;” Jer. 49:1, 3, R.V.; Zeph. 1:5), the national idol of the Ammonites. When Rabbah was taken by David, the crown of this idol was among the spoils. The weight is said to have been “a talent of gold” (above 100 lbs.).

1990.d: King of help, one of the four sons of Saul (1 Chr. 8:33). He perished along with his father in the battle of Gilboa (1 Sam. 31:2).

1906.d: A priest who stood by Ezra when he “read in the book of the law of God” (Neh. 8:4).

1910.d: The head of the fifth division of the priests in the time of David (1 Chr. 24:9).

1914.d: One of the priests appointed as musicians to celebrate the completion of the walls of Jerusalem (Neh. 12:42).

1916.d: Reigning, the personal servant or slave of the high priest Caiaphas. He is mentioned only by John. Peter cut off his right ear in the garden of Gethsemane (John 18:10). But our Lord cured it with a touch (Matt. 26:51; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:51).

1917.d: My fulness, a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman the Levite (1 Chr. 25:4), and chief of the nineteenth division of the temple musicians (26).

1918.d: A Levite of the family of Merari (1 Chr. 6:44).

1921.d: A priest who returned from Babylon (Neh. 12:2).

1923.d: An Amoritish chief in alliance with Abraham (Gen. 14:13, 24).

1926.d: Consoler, a Christian teacher at Antioch. Nothing else is known of him beyond what is stated in Acts 13:1, where he is spoken of as having been brought up with (Gr. syntrophos; rendered in R.V.

1928.d: The elder of the two sons of Joseph. He and his brother Ephraim were afterwards adopted by Jacob as his own sons (48:1). There is an account of his marriage to a Syrian (1 Chr. 7:14)

1930.d: The only son and successor of Hezekiah on the throne of Judah. He was twelve years old when he began to reign (2 Kings 21:1), and he reigned fifty-five years (B.C. 698-643). Though he reigned so long, yet comparatively little is known of this king.

1933.d: Rest, a Danite, the father of Samson (Judg. 13:1-22, and 14:2-4).

1679.d: The evangelist; “John whose surname was Mark” (Acts 12:12, 25). Mark (Marcus, Col. 4:10, etc.) was his Roman name, which gradually came to supersede his Jewish name John. He is called John in Acts 13:5, 13, and Mark in 15:39, 2 Tim. 4:11, etc.
1679.e: First missionary journey begins, Barnabas and Saul go to Cyprus, Mission to Antioch in Pisidia, Paul and Barnabas part ways

1937.d: Bitterness, the sister of Lazarus and Mary, and probably the eldest of the family, who all resided at Bethany (Luke 10:38, 40, 41; John 11:1-39).

1938.d: The wife of Joseph, the mother of Jesus, called the “Virgin Mary,” though never so designated in Scripture (Matt. 2:11; Acts 1:14). Little is known of her personal history. Her genealogy is given in Luke 3.

1939.d: Mary the sister of Lazarus is brought to our notice in connection with the visits of our Lord to Bethany.

1941.d: Mary the mother of John Mark was one of the earliest of our Lord’s disciples. She was the sister of Barnabas (Col. 4:10), and joined with him in disposing of their land and giving the proceeds of the sale into the treasury of the Church (Acts 4:37; 12:12).
1941.e: An angel rescues Peter from prison

1942.d: A Christian at Rome who treated Paul with special kindness (Rom. 16:6).

1943.d: A surname derived from Magdala, the place of her nativity, given to one of the Marys of the Gospels to distinguish her from the other Marys (Matt. 27:56, 61; 28:1, etc.).

1944.d: (= Meshech 1 Chr. 1:17), one of the four sons of Aram, and the name of a tribe descended from him (Gen. 10:23) inhabiting some part probably of Mesopotamia.

1945.d: A lifting up, gift, one of the sons of Ishmael, the founder of an Arabian tribe (Gen. 25:14); a nomad tribe inhabiting the Arabian desert toward Babylonia.

1948.d: A priest of Baal, slain before his altar during the reformation under Jehoiada (2 Kings 11:18).

1952.d: A Levite, son of Heman, the chief of the ninth class of temple singers (1 Chr. 25:4, 16).

1954.d: A Levite who assisted in purifying the temple at the reformation under Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29:13).

1963.d: The son of Amos, in the genealogy of our Lord (Luke 3:25).

1964.d: The son of Semei, in the same genealogy (Luke 3:26).

1968.d: The son of Eleazar, and father of Jacob, who was the father of Joseph, the husband of the Virgin Mary (Matt. 1:15).

1969.d: The son of Levi, and father of Heli (Luke 3:24).

1971.d: Gift of God, a common Jewish name after the Exile. He was the son of Alphaeus, and was a publican or tax-gatherer at Capernaum.

1973.d: The eldest son of Shallum, of the family of Korah (1 Chr. 9:31).

1974.d: One of the sons of Jeduthun (1 Chr. 25:3, 21).

1976.d: One who stood by Ezra while reading the law (Neh. 8:4).

1978.d: Contention, the third son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen. 25:2).

1979.d: Whose benefactor is God, the father of Delaiah, and grandfather of Shemaiah, who joined Sanballat against Nehemiah (Neh. 6:10).

1980.d: Wife of Hadad, one of the kings of Edom (Gen. 36:39).

1983.d: Smitten by God, the son of Irad, and father of Methusael (Gen. 4:18).

1984.d: Faithful, one of the eunchs whom Ahasuerus (Xerxes) commanded to bring in Vashti (Esther 1:10).

1985.d: Habitations, (2 Chr. 26:7; R.V. “Meunim,” Vulg. Ammonitae), a people against whom Uzziah waged a successful war. This word is in Hebrew the plural of Ma’on, and thus denotes the Maonites who inhabited the country on the eastern side of the Wady el-Arabah.

1988.d: The son of Addi, and father of Neri (Luke 3:28).

1991.d: King of righteousness, the king of Salem (q.v.). All we know of him is recorded in Gen. 14:18-20. He is subsequently mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Ps. 110:4.

1992.d: Fulness, the son of Menan and father of Eliakim, in the genealogy of our Lord (Luke 3:31).

1993.d: King, the second of Micah’s four sons (1 Chr. 8:35), and thus grandson of Mephibosheth.

1994.d: Probably a Persian word meaning master of wine, i.e., chief butler; the title of an officer at the Babylonian court (Dan. 1:11, 16) who had charge of the diet of the Hebrew youths.

1995.d: Dignified, one of the royal counsellors at the court of Ahasuerus, by whose suggestion Vashti was divorced (Esther 1:14, 16, 21).

1996.d: Conforting, the son of Gadi, and successor of Shallum, king of Israel, whom he slew. After a reign of about ten years (B.C. 771-760) he died, leaving the throne to his son Pekahiah. His reign was one of cruelty and oppression (2 Kings 15:14-22).

1999.d: The son of Jonathan, and grandson of Saul (2 Sam. 4:4). He was but five years old when his father and grandfather fell on Mount Gilboa.

2000.d: The name of Saul’s son by the concubine Rizpah (q.v.), the daughter of Aiah. He and his brother Armoni were with five others “hanged on a hill before the Lord” by the Gibeonites, and their bodies exposed in the sun for five months (2 Sam. 21:8-10).

2001.d: Increase, the eldest of Saul’s two daughters (1 Sam. 14:49). She was betrothed to David after his victory over Goliath, but does not seem to have entered heartily into this arrangement (18:2, 17, 19).

2002.d: Resistance, a chief priest, a contemporary of the high priest Joiakim (Neh. 12:12).

2003.d: Father of Amariah, a high priest of the line of Eleazar (1 Chr. 6:6, 7, 52).

2004.d: Sad; bitter, the youngest son of Levi, born before the descent of Jacob into Egypt, and one of the seventy who accompanied him thither (Gen. 46:11; Ex. 6:16). He became the head of one of the great divisions of the Levites (Ex. 6:19).

2005.d: Rebellion, one of the sons of Ezra, of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr. 4:17).

2006.d: Exaltations, heights, a priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:3), to whom were sent the sacred vessels (Ezra 8:33) belonging to the temple. He took part in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem (Neh. 3:4).

2009.d: Heb. id, a king of Moab, the son of Chemosh-Gad, a man of great wealth in flocks and herds (2 Kings 3:4). After the death of Ahab at Ramoth-Gilead, Mesha shook off the yoke of Israel

2010.d: Heb. meysh’a, “deliverance,” the eldest son of Caleb (1 Chr. 2:42), and brother of Jerahmeel.

2092.d: One of the three Hebrew youths who were trained with Daniel in Babylon (Dan. 1:11, 19), and promoted to the rank of Magi.

2012.d: Drawing out, the sixth son of Japheth (Gen. 10:2), the founder of a tribe (1 Chr. 1:5; Ezek. 27:13; 38:2, 3). They were in all probability the Moschi, a people inhabiting the Moschian Mountains, between the Black and the Caspian Seas. In Ps.

2013.d: Friendship of Jehovah, a Levite of the family of the Korhites, called also Shelemiah (1 Chr. 9:21; 26:1, 2, 9, 14). He was a temple gate-keeper in the time of David.

2017.d: A priest, the son of Immer (Neh. 11:13).

2020.d: Grandfather of Shaphan, “the scribe,” in the reign of Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).

2022.d: One of the chief Gadites in Bashan in the time of Jotham (1 Chr. 5:13).

2033.d: One of the principal Israelites who supported Ezra when expounding the law to the people (Neh. 8:4).

2040.d: Friend, the wife of Manasseh, and the mother of Amon (2 Kings 21:19), Kings of Judah.

2041.d: Champion of El; man of God, a descendant of Cain (Gen. 4:18), so called, perhaps, to denote that even among the descendants of Cain God had not left himself without a witness.

2042.d: Man of the dart, the son of Enoch, and grandfather of Noah. He was the oldest man of whom we have any record, dying at the age of nine hundred and sixty-nine years, in the year of the Flood (Gen. 5:21-27; 1 Chr. 1:3).

2043.d: Water of gold, the father of Matred (Gen. 36:39; 1 Chr. 1:50), and grandfather of Mehetabel, wife of Hadar, the last king of Edom.

2045.d: Choice, a Hagarene, one of David’s warriors (1 Chr. 11:38); called also Bani the Gadite (2 Sam. 23:36).

2046.d: One of Ishmael’s twelve sons, and head of an Arab tribe (Gen. 25:13).

2048.d: Fortress, one of the Edomitish “dukes” descended from Esau (Gen. 36:42; 1 Chr. 1:53).

2049.d: A man of Mount Ephraim, whose history so far is introduced in Judg.

2050.d: A descendant of Joel the Reubenite (1 Chr. 5:5).

2053.d: “The Morasthite,” so called to distinguish him from Micaiah, the son of Imlah (1 Kings 22:8). He was a prophet of Judah, a contemporary of Isaiah (Micah 1:1), a native of Moresheth of Gath (1:14, 15). Very little is known of the circumstances of his life (comp.

2054.d: Who is like Jehovah?, the son of Imlah, a faithful prophet of Samaria (1 Kings 22:8-28).

2051.d: The son of Zabdi, a Levite of the family of Asaph (Neh. 11:17, 22).

2058.d: The father of Sethur, the spy selected to represent Asher (Num. 13:13).

2059.d: A chief Gadite in Bashan (1 Chr. 5:13).

2062.d: 1 Chr. 7:3, a chief of the tribe of Issachar.

2064.d: A Manassite, “a captain of thousands” who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:20).

2066.d: One of the sons of king Jehoshaphat (2 Chr. 21:2, 4). He was murdered by his brother Jehoram.

2068.d: The title given to one of the chief angels (Dan. 10:13, 21; 12:1). He had special charge of Israel as a nation. He disputed with Satan (Jude 1:9) about the body of Moses.

2052.d: The first in rank of the priests of the family of Kohathites (1 Chr. 23:20).

2070.d: One of those sent out by Jehoshaphat to instruct the people in the law (2 Chr. 17:7).

2072.d: The son of Gemariah. He reported to the king’s officers Jeremiah’s prediction, which he had heard Baruch read (Jer. 36:11, 13) from his father Gemariah’s chamber in the temple.

2073.d: Rivulet, or who as God?, the younger of Saul’s two daughters by his wife Ahinoam (1 Sam. 14:49, 50). “Attracted by the graces of his person and the gallantry of his conduct, she fell in love with David and became his wife” (18:20-28).

2074.d: Prize of Jehovah, a Benjamite, the father of Uzzi (1 Chr. 9:8).

2075.d: Strife, the fourth son of Abraham by Keturah, the father of the Midianites (Gen. 25:2; 1 Chr. 1:32).

2079.d: An officer under Dodai, in the time of David and Solomon (1 Chr. 27:4).

2081.d: Eloquent, a Levitical musician (Neh. 12:36) who took part in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem.

2077.d: A chief priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:5), called Mijamin (10:7) and Miniamin (12:17).

2087.d: The sister of Moses and Aaron (Ex. 2:4-10; 1 Chr. 6:3). Her name is prominent in the history of the Exodus. She is called “the prophetess” (Ex. 15:20). She took the lead in the song of triumph after the passage of the Red Sea.

2088.d: 1 Chr. 4:17, one of the descendants of Judah.

2090.d: A Levite; the eldest of the three sons of Uzziel (Ex. 6:22).

2093.d: Their cleansing or their beholding, a Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal (1 Chr. 8:12).

2094.d: One of the sons of Ishmael (Gen. 25:14), and founder of an Arab tribe.

2096.d: Fatness, one of the Gadite heroes who gathered to David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:10).

2099.d: Number, one of the Jews who accompanied Zerubbabel from Babylon (Ezra 2:2); called also Mispereth (Neh. 7:7).

2100.d: The dual form of matzor, meaning a “mound” or “fortress,” the name of a people descended from Ham (Gen. 10:6, 13; 1 Chr. 1:8, 11).

2102.d: Reminding, or remembrancer, a Christian of Jerusalem with whom Paul lodged (Acts 21:16). He was apparently a native of Cyprus, like Barnabas (11:19, 20), and was well known to the Christians of Caesarea (4:36).

2103.d: Used to denote the people of Moab (Num. 22:3-14; Judg. 3:30; 2 Sam. 8:2; Jer. 48:11, 13).

2104.d: King, the name of the national god of the Ammonites, to whom children were sacrificed by fire. He was the consuming and destroying and also at the same time the purifying fire.

2107.d: The son of Jair, of the tribe of Benjamin. It has been alleged that he was carried into captivity with Jeconiah, and hence that he must have been at least one hundred and twenty-nine years old in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus (Xerxes).

2108.d: Drawn (or Egypt. mesu, “son;” hence Rameses, royal son). On the invitation of Pharaoh (Gen. 45:17-25), Jacob and his sons went down into Egypt. This immigration took place probably about 350 years before the birth of Moses.

2111.n: Mother of the Wife of Simon

2113.d: One of the sons of Caleb (1 Chr. 2:46).

2114.d: The son of Zimri, of the posterity of Saul (1 Chr. 8:36, 37; 9:42, 43).

2116.d: Receding, the second of the two sons of Merari (Ex. 6:19; Num. 3:20). His sons were called Mushites (Num. 3:33; 26:58).

2117.d: Pleasantness, one of the three sons of Caleb, the son of Jephunneh (1 Chr. 4:15).

2118.d: The daughter of Lamech and Zillah (Gen. 4: 22).

2119.d: The daughter of the king of Ammon, one of the wives of Solomon, the only one who appears to have borne him a son, viz., Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:21, 31).

2122.d: Pleasantness, a Syrian, the commander of the armies of Benhadad II. in the time of Joram, king of Israel. He was afflicted with leprosy

2124.d: A girl, the second of Ashur’s two wives, of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr. 4:5, 6).

2125.d: Youthful, a military chief in David’s army (1 Chr. 11:37), called also Paarai (2 Sam. 23:35).

2126.d: Foolish, a descendant of Caleb who dwelt at Maon (1 Sam. 25), the modern Main, 7 miles south-east of Hebron.

2127.d: Fruits, “the Jezreelite,” was the owner of a portion of ground on the eastern slope of the hill of Jezreel (2 Kings 9:25, 26). This small “plat of ground” seems to have been all he possessed.

2170.d: Moved of Jehovah, one of the sons of Jeconiah (1 Chr. 3:18).

2172.d: The son of Hachaliah (Neh. 1:1), and probably of the tribe of Judah. His family must have belonged to Jerusalem (Neh. 2:3).

2174.d: Copper, the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem, and the wife of Jehoiakin (2 Kings 24:8), king of Judah.

2177.d: A Reubenite, a son of Eliab, and brother of Dathan and Abiram (Num. 26:9).

2190.d: A priest who blew the trumpet before the ark when it was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 15:24).

2192.d: A temple porter, of the family of the Korhites (1 Chr. 26:4).

2220.d: A Gadite who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:9).

2223.d: A Levite who superintended the repairs of the temple under Josiah (2 Chr. 34:12).

2224.d: One who accompanied Ezra on the return from Babylon (Ezra 8:9).

2228.d: A son of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:21, 22), and the grandfather of David (Matt. 1:5).
