2443.d: A crusher, Gomer’s second son (Gen. 10:3), supposed to have been the ancestor of the Paphlagonians.

2444.d: Coal; hot stone, the daughter of Aiah, and one of Saul’s concubines. She was the mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth (2 Sam. 3:7; 21:8, 10, 11).

2446.d: Elevation of help, one of the sons of Heman, “the king’s seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn.” He was head of the “four-and-twentieth” course of singers (1 Chr. 25:4, 31).

2450.d: A friend, a Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, whose father, Elimelech, had settled in the land of Moab.

2451.d: Rest, the third son of Cush (Gen. 10:7; 1 Chr. 1:9).

2453.d: A son of Obed-edom the Gittite, and a temple porter (1 Chr. 26:4).

2454.d: Just, mentioned in the genealogy of our Lord (Matt. 1:14).

2455.d: A shoot, a descendant of Arphaxed (Luke 3:35, 36); called also Shelah (1 Chr. 1:18, 24).

2457.d: Whom I asked of God, the son of Jeconiah (Matt. 1:12; 1 Chr. 3:17); also called the son of Neri (Luke 3:27).

2463.d: Shady; or Zalmon (q.v.), a hill covered with dark forests, south of Shechem, from which Abimelech and his men gathered wood to burn that city (Judg. 9:48). In Ps.

2464.d: The wife of Zebedee and mother of James and John (Mat. 27:56), and probably the sister of Mary, the mother of our Lord (John 19:25). She sought for her sons places of honour in Christ’s kingdom (Matt. 20:20, 21; comp. 19:28).

2466.d: Be gracious, O Nebo! or a cup-bearer of Nebo, probably the title of Nergal-sharezer, one of the princes of Babylon (Jer. 39:3).

2468.d: Of the sun, the son of Manoah, born at Zorah. The narrative of his life is given in Judg. 13-16. He was a “Nazarite unto God” from his birth, the first Nazarite mentioned in Scripture (Judg. 13:3-5; comp. Num. 6:1-21).

2469.d: Heard of God. The peculiar circumstances connected with his birth are recorded in 1 Sam. 1:20. Hannah, one of the two wives of Elkanah, who came up to Shiloh to worship before the Lord, earnestly prayed to God that she might become the mother of a son.

2470.d: Held some place of authority in Samaria when Nehemiah went up to Jerusalem to rebuild its ruined walls. He vainly attempted to hinder this work (Neh. 2:10, 19; 4:1-12; 6).

2472.d: Beautiful, the wife of Ananias (q.v.). She was a partner in his guilt and also in his punishment (Acts 5:1-11).
2472.e: Ananias and Sapphira lie to God

2473.d: Princess, the wife and at the same time the half-sister of Abraham (Gen. 11:29; 20:12). This name was given to her at the time that it was announced to Abraham that she should be the mother of the promised child.
2473.e: Abraham is called to Canaan, Abraham goes to Egypt

2476.d: Adversary; accuser. When used as a proper name, the Hebrew word so rendered has the article “the adversary” (Job 1:6-12; 2:1-7). In the New Testament it is used as interchangeable with Diabolos, or the devil, and is so used more than thirty times.
2476.e: Ananias and Sapphira lie to God, Man falls into sin

2478.d: The son of Kish (probably his only son, and a child of prayer, “asked for”), of the tribe of Benjamin, the first king of the Jewish nation. The singular providential circumstances connected with his election as king are recorded in 1 Sam. 8-10.

2480.d: An implement, a Jew, chief of the priests at Ephesus (Acts 19:13-16); i.e., the head of one of the twenty-four courses of the house of Levi.

2481.d: One of the sons of Cush (Gen. 10:7).

2482.d: Second, a Christian of Thessalonica who accompanied Paul into Asia (Acts 20:4).

2483.d: The youngest son of Hiel the Bethelite. His death is recorded in 1 Kings 16:34 (comp. Josh. 6:26).

2485.d: A Horite; one of the “dukes” of Edom (Gen. 36:20-30).

2488.d: Mentioned in the genealogy of our Lord (Luke 3:26).

2489.d: Sin (the god) sends many brothers, son of Sargon, whom he succeeded on the throne of Assyria (B.C. 705), in the 23rd year of Hezekiah.

2491.d: Barley, the chief of the forth priestly course (1 Chr. 24:8).

2492.d: Abundance; princess, the daughter of Asher and grand-daughter of Jacob (Gen. 46:17); called also Sarah (Num. 26:46; R.V., “Serah”).

2498.d: A priest of the days of Jehoiakim (Neh. 12:1, 12).

2500.d: The son of Neriah. When Zedekiah made a journey to Babylon to do homage to Nebuchadnezzar, Seraiah had charge of the royal gifts to be presented on that occasion.

2501.d: Fear, one of the sons of Zebulun (Gen. 46:14).

2502.d: A “prudent man” (R.V., “man of understanding”), the deputy (R.V., “proconsul”) of Cyprus (Acts 13:6-13). He became a convert to Christianity under Paul, who visited this island on his first mission to the heathen.
2502.e: Barnabas and Saul go to Cyprus

2503.d: Branch, the father of Nahor (Gen. 11:20-23); called Saruch in Luke 3:35.

2504.d: Appointed; a substitute, the third son of Adam and Eve (Gen. 4:25; 5:3). His mother gave him this name, “for God,” said she, “hath appointed me [i.e., compensated me with] another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.”

2505.d: Hidden, one of the spies sent to search the Promised Land. He was of the tribe of Asher (Num. 13:13).

2508.d: Servant of the beautiful, a chief eunuch in the second house of the harem of king Ahasuerus (Esther 2:14).

1398.d: Aku’s command, the Chaldean name given to Hananiah, one of the Hebrew youths whom Nebuchadnezzar carried captive to Babylon (Dan. 1:6, 7; 3:12-30).

2514.d: The son of Jabesh, otherwise unknown. He “conspired against Zachariah, and smote him before the people, and slew him, and reigned in his stead” (2 Kings 15:10). He reigned only “a month of days in Samaria” (15:13, marg.).

2515.d: Keeper of the temple vestments in the reign of Josiah (2 Kings 22:14).

2517.d: One of the posterity of Judah (1 Chr. 2:40, 41).

2520.d: A keeper of the gate in the reign of David (1 Chr. 9:17).

2525.d: The uncle of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. 32:7).

2529.d: An Assyrian king (Hos. 10:14), identified with Shalmaneser II. (Sayce) or IV. (Lenormant), the successor of Pul on the throne of Assyria (B.C. 728). He made war against Hoshea, the king of Israel, whom he subdued and compelled to pay an annual tribute.

2725.d: A man of Asher (1 Chr. 7:32); called also Shamer (34).

2534.d: The Philistines from the maritime plain had made incursions into the Hebrew upland for the purposes of plunder, when one of this name, the son of Anath, otherwise unknown, headed a rising for the purpose of freeing the land from this oppression.

2536.d: One of the sons of Michah (1 Chr. 24:24).

2539.d: One of David’s three mighty men (2 Sam. 23:11, 12).

2540.d: One of David’s mighties (2 Sam. 23:25); called also Shammoth (1 Chr. 11:27) and Shamhuth (27:8).

2700.d: One of the sons of Jesse (1 Sam. 16:9). He is also called Shimeah (2 Sam. 13:3) and Shimma (1 Chr. 2:13).

2545.d: One of the spies sent out by Moses to search the land (Num. 13:4). He represented the tribe of Reuben.

2547.d: One of David’s sons by Bathsheba (1 Chr. 3:5); called also Shammua (14:4).

2550.d: A coney, a scribe or secretary of king Josiah (2 Kings 22:3-7). He consulted Huldah concerning the newly-discovered copy of the law which was delivered to him by Hilkiah the priest (8-14). His grandson Gedaliah was governor of Judea (25:22).

2552.d: One of the spies. He represented the tribe of Simeon (Num. 13:5).

2556.d: One of David’s chief herdsmen (1 Chr. 27:29).

2558.d: One of David’s heroes (1 Chr. 11:35); called also Sharar (2 Sam. 23:33).

2559.d: (god) protect the king!, a son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria. He and his brother Adrammelech murdered their father, and then fled into the land of Armenia (2 Kings 19:37).

2477.d: A king of Edom (Gen. 36:37, 38); called Shaul in 1 Chr. 1:48.

2493.d: (“Seraiah,” 2 Sam. 8:17; “Shisha,” 1 Kings 4:3), one of David’s secretaries (1 Chr. 18:16).

2456.d: Asked for of God, father of Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2, 8; Neh. 12:1).

2567.d: Heb. shebha, the son of Raamah (Gen. 10:7), whose descendants settled with those of Dedan on the Persian Gulf.

2568.d: Heb. id. A son of Joktan (Gen. 10:28), probably the founder of the Sabeans.

2569.d: Heb. id. A son of Jokshan, who was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen. 25:3).

2570.d: Heb. id. A “son of Bichri,” of the family of Becher, the son of Benjamin, and thus of the stem from which Saul was descended (2 Sam. 20:1-22).

2572.d: A Levite appointed to blow the trumpet before the ark of God (1 Chr. 15:24).

2574.d: A priest who returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:3; marg., or Shebaniah).

2577.d: Tender youth, “treasurer” over the house in the reign of Hezekiah, i.e., comptroller or governor of the palace. On account of his pride he was ejected from his office, and Eliakim was promoted to it (Isa. 22:15-25).

2581.d: A priest to whom the tenth lot came forth when David divided the priests (1 Chr. 24:11).

2582.d: One of the priests who were set “to give to their brethren by courses” of the daily portion (2 Chr. 31:15). Shechani’ah, id.

2583.d: A priest whose sons are mentioned in 1 Chr. 3:21, 22.

2586.d: The father of Shemaiah, who repaired the wall of Jerusalem (Neh. 3:29).

2588.d: The son of Hamor the Hivite (Gen. 33:19; 34).

2600.d: Father of one of those who accused Jeremiah to Zedekiah (Jer. 37:3; 38:1).

2601.d: Father of a captain of the ward (Jer. 37:13).

2613.d: A name; renown, the first mentioned of the sons of Noah (Gen. 5:32; 6:10). He was probably the eldest of Noah’s sons. The words “brother of Japheth the elder” in Gen. 10:21 are more correctly rendered “the elder brother of Japheth,” as in the Revised Version.
2613.e: The Great Flood begins, Water covers the earth, The flood subsides, Leaving the Ark, Noah gets drunk and Canaan is cursed

2617.d: One who stood by Ezra when he read the law (Neh. 8:4).

2618.d: Rumour, a Benjamite whose sons “came to David to Ziklag” (1 Chr. 12:3).

2619.d: A prophet in the reign of Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:22-24).

2625.d: A Levite in the time of David, who with 200 of his brethren took part in the bringing up of the ark from Obed-edom to Hebron (1 Chr. 15:8).

2627.d: The eldest son of Obed-edom (1 Chr. 26:4-8).

2628.d: One of the Levites whom Jehoshaphat appointed to teach the law (2 Chr. 17:8).

2630.d: A Levite appointed to “distribute the oblations of the Lord” (2 Chr. 31:15).

2637.d: A false prophet who hindered the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Neh. 6:10).

2642.d: The father of Urijah the prophet (Jer. 26:20).

2643.d: A false prophet who opposed Jeremiah (Jer. 29:24-32).

2644.d: The father of a prince in the reign of Jehoiakim (Jer. 36:12).

2645.d: One who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:5).

2648.d: Soaring on high, the king of Zeboiim, who joined with the other kings in casting off the yoke of Chedorlaomer. After having been reconquered by him, he was rescued by Abraham (Gen. 14:2).

2651.d: A Levite in David’s time (1 Chr. 15:18, 20).

2652.d: A Levite in the reign of Jehoshaphat (2 Chr. 17:8).

2653.d: The son of Ammihud. He represented Simeon in the division of the land (Num. 34:20).

2654.d: A prince of the tribe of Issachar (1 Chr. 7:2).

2658.d: A Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:5).

2659.d: A Simeonite prince in David’s time (1 Chr. 27:16).

2664.d: One of the princes who urged the putting of Jeremiah to death (Jer. 38:1-4).

2669.d: Root, a descendant of Manasseh (1 Chr. 7:16).

2670.d: One of the messengers whom the children of the Captivity sent to Jerusalem “to pray for them before the Lord” (Zech. 7:2).

2673.d: A star, a prince at the court of Ahasuerus (Esther 1:14).

2674.d: Star of splendour, a Persian officer who vainly attempted to hinder the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 5:3, 6; 6:6, 13).

2680.d: A Levite of the family of Merari (1 Chr. 6:30).

2681.d: Another Levite of the family of Gershon (1 Chr. 6:39).

2682.d: A Benjamite, a descendant of Gibeon (1 Chr. 8:32); called also Shimeam (9:38).

691.d: A Levite of the family of Gershon (1 Chr. 6:42).

2684.d: A Benjamite of the house of Saul, who stoned and cursed David when he reached Bahurim in his flight from Jerusalem on the occasion of the rebellion of Absalom (2 Sam. 16:5-13).

2685.d: One of David’s mighty men who refused to acknowledge Adonijah as David’s successor (1 Kings 1:8). He is probably the same person who is called elsewhere (4:18) “the son of Elah.”

2686.d: A son of Pedaiah, the brother of Zerubbabel (1 Chr. 3:19).

2690.d: A Ramathite who was “over the vineyards” of David (1 Chr. 27:27).

2691.d: One of the sons of Heman, who assisted in the purification of the temple (2 Chr. 29:14).

2704.d: The father of one of the “valiant men” of David’s armies (1 Chr. 11:45).

2705.d: Assisted at the purification of the temple in the time of Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29:13).

2724.d: The mother of Jehozabad, who murdered Joash (2 Kings 12:21); called also Shimrith, a Moabitess (2 Chr. 24:26).

2706.d: Watchman, the fourth son of Issachar (Gen. 46:13; 1 Chr. 7:1; R.V., correctly, “Shimron”).

2707.d: The shining one, or sunny, the secretary of Rehum the chancellor, who took part in opposing the rebuilding of the temple after the Captivity (Ezra 4:8, 9, 17-23).

2708.d: Cooling, the king of Adamah, in the valley of Siddim, who with his confederates was conquered by Chedorlaomer (Gen. 14:2).

2710.d: Beauty, one of the Egyptian midwives (Ex. 1:15).

2711.d: Judicial, an Ephraimite prince at the time of the division of Canaan (Num. 34:24).

2712.d: '=Sheshonk I., king of Egypt. His reign was one of great national success, and a record of his wars and conquests adorns the portico of what are called the “Bubastite kings” at Karnak, the ancient Thebes. Among these conquests is a record of that of Judea.

2715.d: One of David’s sons by Bathseheba (2 Sam. 5:14).

2716.d: One of the sons of Caleb (1 Chr. 2:18), the son of Hezron.

2717.d: Poured out, the “captain of the host of Hadarezer” when he mustered his vassals and tributaries from beyond “the river Euphrates” (2 Sam. 10:15-18); called also Shophach (1 Chr. 19:16).

2719.d: The second son of Seir the Horite; one of the Horite “dukes” (Gen. 36:20).

2720.d: One of the sons of Caleb, and a descendant of Hur (1 Chr. 2:50, 52; 4:1, 2).

2722.d: Captor, son of Nahash of Rabbah, the Ammonite. He showed kindness to David when he fled from Jerusalem to Mahanaim (2 Sam. 17:27).

2726.d: A daughter of Heber the Asherite (1 Chr. 7:32).

2727.d: One of Abraham’s sons by Keturah (Gen. 25:2; Chr. 1:32).

2728.d: A Canaanite whose daughter was married to Judah (1 Chr. 2:3).

2579.d: One of the descendants of Gershom, who had charge of the temple treasures in the time of David (1 Chr. 23:16; 26:24).

2580.d: One of the sons of Heman; one of those whose duty it was to “lift up the horn” in the temple service (1 Chr. 25:4, 5); called also Shubael (ver. 20).

2737.d: The Lord sustains, one of David’s heroes (1 Chr. 11:29), general of the eighth division of the army (27:11). He slew the giant Saph in the battle of Gob (2 Sam. 21:18; R.V., “Sibbechai”). Called also Mebunnai (23:27).

2739.d: Striking down. The whole country on the east of Jordan, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, was possessed by the Amorites, whose king, Sihon, refused to permit the Israelites to pass through his territory, and put his army in array against them.

2740.d: Wood, a prominent member of the church at Jerusalem; also called Silvanus.
2740.e: Jerusalem Council, Second Missionary Journey begins, Paul and Silas imprisoned, Philippian jailer converted, Uproar in Thessalonica, Mission to Berea, "Mission

2741.d: The second son of Jacob by Leah (Gen. 29:33). He was associated with Levi in the terrible act of vengeance against Hamor and the Shechemites (34:25, 26). He was detained by Joseph in Egypt as a hostage (42:24).

2743.d: One of the ancestors of Joseph (Luke 3:30).

2744.d: Surnamed Niger, i.e., “black,” perhaps from his dark complexion, a teacher of some distinction in the church of Antioch (Acts 13:1-3). It has been supposed that this was the Simon of Cyrene who bore Christ’s cross.

2746.d: One of the twelve apostles, called the Canaanite (Matt. 10:4; Mark 3:18). This word “Canaanite” does not mean a native of Canaan, but is derived from the Syriac word Kanean or Kaneniah, which was the name of a Jewish sect.

2747.d: One of the brothers of our Lord (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3).

2748.d: A leper of Bethany, in whose house Mary anointed our Lord’s head with ointment “as he sat at meat” (Matt. 26:6-13; Mark 14:3-9).

2749.d: A Jew of Cyrene, in North Africa, then a province of Libya. A hundred thousand Jews from Palestine had been settled in this province by Ptolemy Soter (B.C. 323-285), where by this time they had greatly increased in number.

2752.d: A sorcerer of great repute for his magical arts among the Samaritans (Acts 8:9-11). He afterwards became a professed convert to the faith under the preaching of Philip the deacon and evangelist (12, 13). His profession was, however, soon found to be hollow.

2753.d: A Christian at Joppa, a tanner by trade, with whom Peter on one occasion lodged (Acts 9:43).
2753.e: Peter heals Aeneas and Dorcas, Peter meets Cornelius

2754.d: Watchman, a Levite of the family of Merari (1 Chr. 26:10).

2755.d: An inhabitant of Sin, near Arka (Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15).

2471.d: Extension, the son of the giant whom Sibbechai slew (2 Sam. 21:18); called also Sippai (1 Chr. 20:4).

2757.d: The captain of Jabin’s army (Judg. 4:2), which was routed and destroyed by the army of Barak on the plain of Esdraelon. After all was lost he fled to the settlement of Heber the Kenite in the plain of Zaanaim.

2758.d: The ancestor of some of the Nethinim who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:53; Neh. 7:55).

2760.d: (Nubian, Sabako), an Ethiopian king who brought Egypt under his sway. He was bribed by Hoshea to help him against the Assyrian monarch Shalmaneser (2 Kings 17:4). This was a return to the policy that had been successful in the reign of Jeroboam I.

2762.d: Peaceful, (Heb. Shelomoh), David’s second son by Bathsheba, i.e., the first after their legal marriage (2 Sam. 12). He was probably born about B.C. 1035 (1 Chr. 22:5; 29:1).

2770.d: The father who saves, probably the same as Sosipater, a kinsman of Paul (Rom. 16:21), a Christian of the city of Berea who accompanied Paul into Asia (Acts 20:4-6).

2772.d: Safe in strength, the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, who was seized and beaten by the mob in the presence of Gallio, the Roman governor, when he refused to proceed against Paul at the instigation of the Jews (Acts 18:12-17).

2774.d: Spike; an ear of corn, a convert at Rome whom Paul salutes (Rom. 16:9).

2801.d: Crown, a member of the church at Corinth, whose family were among those the apostle had baptized (1 Cor. 1:16; 16:15, 17). He has been supposed by some to have been the “jailer of Philippi” (comp. Acts 16:33).

2802.d: One of the seven deacons, who became a preacher of the gospel. He was the first Christian martyr. His personal character and history are recorded in Acts 6. “He fell asleep” with a prayer for his persecutors on his lips (7:60).
2802.e: Seven chosen to serve, Stephen is seized, Stephen is stoned, Stephen addresses the council, Saul persecutes the church

2804.d: Lily, with other pious women, ministered to Jesus (Luke 8:3).

2805.d: The father of Gaddi, who was one of the twelve spies (Num. 13:11).

2806.d: Fortunate; affable, a female member of the church at Philippi, whom Paul beseeches to be of one mind with Euodias (Phil. 4:2, 3).

2807.d: Impressions; rings, “the children of,” returned from the Captivity (Ezra 2:43).

2808.d: Goodness of God, the father of one whom the kings of Syria and Samaria in vain attempted to place on the throne of Ahaz (Isa. 7:6).

2809.d: A Persian governor of Samaria, who joined others in the attempt to prevent the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:7).

2811.d: Good is Rimmon, the father of Benhadad, king of Syria (1 Kings 15:18).

2817.d: The wife of Pharaoh, who gave her sister in marriage to Hadad the Edomite (1 Kings 11:19, 20).

2818.d: One of the Anakim of Hebron, who were slain by the men of Judah under Caleb (Num. 13:22; Josh. 15:14; Judg. 1:10).

2819.d: A king of Geshur, to whom Absalom fled after he had put Amnon to death (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37). His daughter, Maachah, was one of David’s wives, and the mother of Absalom (1 Chr. 3:2).

2821.d: The daughter-in-law of Judah, to whose eldest son, Er, she was married (Gen. 38:6). After her husband’s death, she was married to Onan, his brother (8), and on his death, Judah promised to her that his third son, Shelah, would become her husband.

2822.d: A daughter of David (2 Sam. 13:1-32; 1 Chr.

2824.d: Consolation, a Netophathite; one of the captains who supported Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:23; Jer. 40:8).

2828.d: One of the “sons” of Javan (Gen. 10:4; 1 Chr. 1:7).

2830.d: One of Sennacherib’s messengers to Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:17).

2831.d: Gift, a Persian governor (Heb. pehah, i.e., “satrap;” modern “pasha”) “on this side the river”, i.e., of the whole tract on the west of the Euphrates. This Hebrew title pehah is given to governors of provinces generally.

2840.d: One of the sons of Ashur, the father of Tekoa (1 Chr. 4:6).

2841.d: The wanderer; loiterer, for some unknown reason emigrated with his family from his native mountains in the north to the plains of Mesopotamia. He had three sons, Haran, Nahor, and Abraham, and one daughter, Sarah.

2842.d: Severe, a eunuch or chamberlain in the palace of Ahasuerus, who conspired with another to murder him. The plot was detected by Mordecai, and the conspirators were put to death (Esther 2:21; 6:2).

2844.d: A modification of “Tertius;” a Roman advocate, whom the Jews employed to state their case against Paul in the presence of Felix (Acts 24:1-9).

2845.d: A badger, a son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother (Gen. 22:24).

2848.d: Heb. ‘Anakim (Deut. 2:10, 11, 21; Josh. 11:21, 22; 14:12, 15; called “sons of Anak,” Num. 13:33; “children of Anak,” 13:22; Josh. 15:14), a nomad race of giants descended from Arba (Josh.

2849.d: Lover of God, a Christian, probably a Roman, to whom Luke dedicated both his Gospel (Luke 1:3) and the Acts of the Apostles (1:1). Nothing beyond this is known of him.

2850.d: Thanksgiving, referred to by Gamaliel in his speech before the council at Jerusalem (Acts 5:36). He headed an insurrection against the Roman authority. Beyond this nothing is known of him.

2851.d: Twin, one of the twelve (Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18, etc.). He was also called Didymus (John 11:16; 20:24), which is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew name. All we know regarding him is recorded in the fourth Gospel (John 11:15, 16; 14:4, 5; 20:24, 25, 26-29).

2852.d: I.e., as known in Roman history, Tiberius Claudius Nero, only mentioned in Luke 3:1. He was the stepson of Augustus, whom he succeeded on the throne, A.D. 14. He was noted for his vicious and infamous life.

2853.d: Building of Jehovah, the son of Ginath, a man of some position, whom a considerable number of the people chose as monarch.

2854.d: (in the LXX. called “Thorgal”), styled the “king of nations” (Gen. 14:1-9). Mentioned as Tudkhula on Arioch’s brick (see facing page 139). Goyyim, translated “nations,” is the country called Gutium, east of Tigris and north of Elam.

2376.d: An Assyrian king. It has been a question whether he was identical with Tiglath-pileser III. (q.v.), or was his predecessor. The weight of evidence is certainly in favour of their identity.

2858.d: Defiled, the father of blind Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46).

2862.d: Honouring, one of the seven deacons at Jerusalem (Acts 6:5). Nothing further is known of him.

2863.d: Honouring God, a young disciple who was Paul’s companion in many of his journeyings. His mother, Eunice, and his grandmother, Lois, are mentioned as eminent for their piety (2 Tim. 1:5). We know nothing of his father but that he was a Greek (Acts 16:1).
2863.e: Timothy Joins Paul and Silas, Mission to Berea, "Mission to Corinth, 1&2 Thess Written", Mission to Ephesus/1 Cor Written, Mission to Macedonia and Greece, "Mis

2864.d: The youngest of the sons of Japheth (Gen. 10:2; 1 Chr. 1:5).

2865.d: The last king of Egypt of the Ethiopian (the fifteenth) dynasty. He was the brother-in-law of So (q.v.). He probably ascended the throne about B.C. 692, having been previously king of Ethiopia (2 Kings 19:9; Isa. 37:9), which with Egypt now formed one nation.

2868.d: The youngest of Zelophehad’s five daughters (Num. 26:33; Josh. 17:3).

2869.d: Honourable, was with Paul and Barnabas at Antioch, and accompanied them to the council at Jerusalem (Gal. 2:1-3; Acts 15:2), although his name nowhere occurs in the Acts of the Apostles.

2870.d: Good is Jehovah, my Lord, a Levite sent out by Jehoshaphat to instruct the people of Judah in the law (2 Chr. 17:8).

2872.d: Pleasing to Jehovah, the “servant,” the “Ammonite,” who joined with those who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the Exile (Neh. 2:10).

2873.d: Id., a Levite sent out through Judah by Jehoshaphat to teach the people (2 Chr. 17:8).

2875.d: A son of Gomer, and grandson of Japheth (Gen. 10:3).

2877.d: A king of Hamath, who sent “Joram his son unto King David to salute him,” when he “heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer” (2 Sam. 8:9, 10). Called Tou (1 Chr. 18:9, 10).

2879.d: A judge of the tribe of Issachar who “judged” Israel twenty-three years (Judg. 10:1, 2), when he died, and was buried in Shamir. He was succeeded by Jair.

2880.d: A foster-child, an Ephesian who accompanied Paul during a part of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4; 21:29).
2880.e: Mission to Macedonia and Greece, Paul arrested in the Temple

2884.d: The son of Lamech and Zillah, “an instructor of every artificer in brass and iron” (Gen. 4:22; R.V., “the forger of every cutting instrument of brass and iron”).

2885.d: Chance, an Asiatic Christian, a “faithful minister in the Lord” (Eph. 6:21, 22), who, with Trophimus, accompanied Paul on a part of his journey from Macedonia to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). He is alluded to also in Col. 4:7, Titus 3:12, and 2 Tim.

2886.d: Prince, a Greek rhetorician, in whose “school” at Ephesus Paul disputed daily for the space of two years with those who came to him (Acts 19:9). Some have supposed that he was a Jew, and that his “school” was a private synagogue.

2887.d: The name of a person to whom Agur’s words are addressed (Prov. 30:1).

2891.d: A Levite whom David appointed to take part in bringing the ark up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom by playing the psaltery on that occasion (1 Chr. 15:18, 20).

2892.d: A Levite who returned with Zerubbabel from the Captivity (Neh. 12:9).

2898.d: A Hittite, the husband of Bathsheba, whom David first seduced, and then after Uriah’s death married.

2900.d: A Kohathite ancestor of the prophet Samuel (1 Chr. 6:36).

2901.d: The chief of the Kohathites at the time when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 15:5, 11).

2902.d: The father of Michaiah, one of Rehoboam’s wives, and mother of Abijah (2 Chr. 13:2).

2899.d: The father of Meremoth, mentioned in Ezra 8:33.

2903.d: A high priest in the time of Ahaz (2 Kings 16:10-16), at whose bidding he constructed an idolatrous altar like one the king had seen at Damascus, to be set up instead of the brazen altar.

2904.d: One of the priests who stood at the right hand of Ezra’s pulpit when he read and expounded the law (Neh. 8:4).

2905.d: A prophet of Kirjath-jearim in the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah (Jer. 26:20-23). He fled into Egypt from the cruelty of the king, but having been brought back he was beheaded and his body “cast into the graves of the common people.”

2908.d: The son of Aram, and grandson of Shem (Gen. 10:23; 1 Chr. 1:17).

2909.d: One of the Horite “dukes” in the land of Edom (Gen. 36:28).

2911.d: A wanderer, a descendant of Joktan (Gen. 10:27; 1 Chr. 1:21), the founder apparently of one of the Arab tribes; the name also probably of the province they occupied and of their chief city.

2916.d: Strength, a son of Abinadab, in whose house the men of Kirjath-jearim placed the ark when it was brought back from the land of the Philistines (1 Sam. 7:1).

2917.d: The son of Bukki, and a descendant of Aaron (1 Chr. 6:5, 51; Ezra 7:4).

2919.d: A son of Bela, and grandson of Benjamin (1 Chr. 7:7).

2920.d: A Benjamite, a chief in the tribe (1 Chr. 9:8).

2921.d: A son of Bani. He had the oversight of the Levites after the return from captivity (Neh. 11:22).

2922.d: The head of the house of Jedaiah, one of “the chief of the priests” (Neh. 12:19).

2923.d: A priest who assisted in the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem (Neh. 12:42).

375.d: One of Amaziah’s sons, whom the people made king of Judah in his father’s stead (2 Kings 14:21; 2 Chr. 26:1).

2926.d: The father of Jehonathan, one of David’s overseers (1 Chr. 27:25).

2929.d: One of the sons of Kohath, and uncle of Aaron (Ex. 6:18; Lev. 10:4).

2931.d: A son of Bela, and grandson of Benjamin (1 Chr. 7:7).

2932.d: One of the sons of Heman (1 Chr. 25:4); called also Azareel (18).

2935.d: Purity; worthy of honour, one of Haman’s sons, whom the Jews slew in the palace of Shushan (Esther 9:9).

2937.d: Beautiful, the queen of Ahasuerus, who was deposed from her royal dignity because she refused to obey the king when he desired her to appear in the banqueting hall of Shushan the palace (Esther 1:10-12).

1746.d: The son of Shemath. He conspired against Joash, king of Judah, and slew him (2 Chr. 24:25, 26). He is called also Jozachar (2 Kings 12:21).

2947.d: One of David’s valiant men (1 Chr. 11:41), the descendant of Ahlai, of the “children of Sheshan” (2:31).

2952.d: The father of Baruch, who “earnestly repaired” part of the wall of Jerusalem (Neh. 3:20; marg., “Zaccai”).

2954.d: An ancestor of Achan (Josh. 7:1, 17, 18). He is probably the “Zimri” of 1 Chr. 2:6.

2956.d: Called “the Shiphmite,” one of David’s officers, who had charge of his vineyards (1 Chr. 27:27).

2957.d: The father of Jashobeam, who was one of David’s officers (1 Chr. 27:2).

2958.d: An overseer of the priests after the Captivity (Neh. 11:14).

2959.d: Gift, the son of Nathan, who was “king’s friend” in the court of Solomon (1 Kings 4:5).

2960.d: Pure, one whose “sons” returned with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:9; Neh. 7:14).

2961.d: Pure, a superintendant of customs; a chief tax-gather (publicanus) at Jericho (Luke 19:1-10).

2963.d: Father of Shammua, who was one of the spies sent out by Moses (Num. 13:4).

2965.d: A son of Asaph, and chief of one of the courses of singers as arranged by David (1 Chr. 25:2, 10).

2969.d: Son of Jeroboam II., king of Israel. On the death of his father there was an interregnum of ten years, at the end of which he succeeded to the throne, which he occupied only six months, having been put to death by Shallum, who usurped the throne.

2971.d: A priest of the course of Abia, the eighth of the twenty-four courses into which the priests had been originally divided by David (1 Chr. 23:1-19). Only four of these courses or “families” of the priests returned from the Exile (Ezra 2:36-39)

3011.d: The son or grandson of Jehoiada, the high priest in the times of Ahaziah and Joash. After the death of Jehoiada he boldly condemned both the king and the people for their rebellion against God (2 Chr.

2972.d: Memorial, a son of Jehiel (1 Chr. 8:31; 9:35); called Zechariah (9:37).

2973.d: A son of Ahitub, of the line of Eleazer (2 Sam. 8:17; 1 Chr. 24:3), high priest in the time of David (2 Sam. 20:25) and Solomon (1 Kings 4:4). He is first mentioned as coming to take part with David at Hebron (1 Chr. 12:27, 28).

2974.d: The father of Jerusha, who was wife of King Uzziah, and mother of King Jotham (2 Kings 15:33; 2 Chr. 27:1).

2976.d: The sons of Baana, one of those who assisted in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem (Neh. 3:4).

2979.d: “The scribe” set over the treasuries of the temple by Nehemiah along with a priest and a Levite (Neh. 13:13).

2983.d: One of the two kings of Midian whom the “Lord delivered” into the hands of Gideon. He was slain afterwards with Zebah (Judg. 8:5-21).

2986.d: Id., one whose descendants returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:8; Neh. 7:13); probably the same as Zatthu.

2944.d: Terror, one of the “dukes of Edom” (Gen. 36:27); called also Zavan (1 Chr. 1:42).

2987.d: Plenty, a descendant of Judah (1 Chr. 2:33).

2991.d: A Korhite porter of the Lord’s house (1 Chr. 26:2). Three or four others of this name are also mentioned.

2992.d: A son of Asahel, Joab’s brother (1 Chr. 27:7).

2993.d: A Levite who took part as one of the teachers in the system of national education instituted by Jehoshaphat (2 Chr. 17:7, 8).

2994.d: The son of Ishmael, “the ruler of the house of Judah in all the king’s matters” (2 Chr. 19:8-11).

2997.d: Man-killer, or sacrifice, one of the two kings who led the vast host of the Midianites who invaded the land of Israel, and over whom Gideon gained a great and decisive victory (Judg. 8).

2998.d: A Galilean fisherman, the husband of Salome (q.v.), and the father of James and John, two of our Lord’s disciples (Matt. 4:21; 27:56; Mark 15:40).

3000.d: Given, the wife of Josiah and mother of Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:36).

3001.d: Habitation, the governor of Shechem under Abimelech (Judg. 9:28, 30, 36). He informed his master of the intention of the people of Shechem to transfer their allegiance to the Hivite tribe of Hamor.

3002.d: Dwelling, the sixth and youngest son of Jacob and Leah (Gen. 30:20). Little is known of his personal history. He had three sons (46:14).

2970.d: The father of Abijah, who was the mother of Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29:1).

3003.d: One of the chiefs of the tribe of Reuben (1 Chr. 5:7).

3004.d: A Levite who assisted at the bringing up of the ark from the house of Obededom (1 Chr. 15:20-24).

3008.d: One who assisted in teaching the law to the people in the time of Jehoshaphat (2 Chr. 17:7).

3009.d: A Levite of the sons of Asaph (2 Chr. 20:14).

3012.d: A prophet, who had “understanding in the seeing of God,” in the time of Uzziah, who was much indebted to him for his wise counsel (2 Chr. 26:5). Besides these, there is a large number of persons mentioned in Scripture bearing this name of whom nothing is known.

3015.d: One of the “rulers of the house of God” (2 Chr. 35:8).

3016.d: A prophet of Judah, the eleventh of the twelve minor prophets. Like Ezekiel, he was of priestly extraction. He describes himself (1:1) as “the son of Berechiah.” In Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 he is called “the son of Iddo,” who was properly his grandfather.

1950.d: The last king of Judah. He was the third son of Josiah, and his mother’s name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, and hence he was the brother of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:31; 24:17, 18). His original name was Mattaniah

3029.d: The son of Chenaanah, a false prophet in the days of Ahab (1 Kings 22:11, 24; 2 Chr. 18:10, 23).

3032.d: The son of Hananiah, a prince of Judah in the days of Jehoiakim (Jer. 36:12).

3033.d: The wolf, one of the two leaders of the great Midianite host which invaded Israel and was utterly routed by Gideon.

3034.d: Cleft, an Ammonite; one of David’s valiant men (2 Sam. 23:37).

3035.d: First-born, of the tribe of Manasseh, and of the family of Gilead; died in the wilderness.

3036.d: The designation of one of the Phoenician tribes (Gen. 10:18) who inhabited the town of Sumra, at the western base of the Lebanon range. In the Amarna tablets (B.C.

3037.d: Vine-dresser, a Benjamite; one of the sons of Becher (1 Chr. 7:8).

3038.d: A disciple called “the lawyer,” whom Paul wished Titus to bring with him (Titus 3:13). Nothing more is known of him.

3039.d: The son of Maaseiah, the “second priest” in the reign of Zedekiah, often mentioned in Jeremiah as having been sent from the king to inquire (Jer.

3041.d: The father of Josiah, the priest who dwelt in Jerusalem when Darius issued the decree that the temple should be rebuilt (Zech. 6:10).

2984.d: A son of Tamar (Gen. 38:30); called also Zara (Matt. 1:3).

3046.d: An “Ethiopian,” probably Osorkon II., the successor of Shishak on the throne of Egypt. With an enormous army, the largest we read of in Scripture, he invaded the kingdom of Judah in the days of Asa (2 Chr. 14:9-15).

3102.d: One of the sons of Simeon (Gen. 46:10; Ex. 6:15).

3049.d: Star of Venus, the wife of Haman, whom she instigated to prepare a gallows for Mordecai (Esther 5:10).

3053.d: Stricken, mother of Jeroboam, the first king of the ten tribes (1 Kings 11:26).

3054.d: The seed of Babylon, the son of Salathiel or Shealtiel (Hag. 1:1; Zorobabel, Matt. 1:12); called also the son of Pedaiah (1 Chr. 3:17-19), i.e., according to a frequent usage of the word “son;” the grandson or the nephew of Salathiel.

3055.d: Stricken of the Lord, David’s sister, and the mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel (1 Chr. 2:16), who were the three leading heroes of David’s army, and being his nephews, they were admitted to the closest companionship with him.

3060.d: Post; statue, “a servant of the house of Saul” (2 Sam. 9:2), who informed David that Mephibosheth, a son of Jonathan, was alive. He afterwards dealt treacherously toward Mephibosheth, whom he slanderously misrepresented to David.

3064.d: The mother of King Joash (2 Kings 12:1; 2 Chr. 24:1).

3067.d: Another of the same tribe (1 Chr. 8:23).

3069.d: A Levite, one of the sons of Asaph (Neh. 11:17); probably the same as Zichri (1 Chr. 9:15), and Zaccur (Neh. 12:35).

3077.d: The Lord is righteous, one who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah (Neh. 10:1).

2738.d: A fishery, a town on the Mediterranean coast, about 25 miles north of Tyre. It received its name from the “first-born” of Canaan, the grandson of Noah (Gen. 10:15, 19).

3078.d: The name of a family of Nethinim (Ezra 2:43; Neh. 7:46).

3080.d: Shadow, one of the wives of Lamech, of the line of Cain, and mother of Tubal-cain (Gen. 4:19, 22).

3081.d: Drooping, Leah’s handmaid, and the mother of Gad and Asher (Gen. 30:9-13).

3083.d: One of the captains of the tribe of Manasseh who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:20).

3086.d: Vine-dressers; celebrated, one of the sons of Abraham by Keturah (Gen. 25:2).

3088.d: Murdered Elah at Tirzah, and succeeded him on the throne of Israel (1 Kings 16:8-10). He reigned only seven days, for Omri, whom the army elected as king, laid siege to Tirzah, whereupon Zimri set fire to the palace and perished amid its ruins (11-20).

3094.d: A little bird, the father of Balak, king of Moab (Num. 22:2, 4).

3095.d: A female bird. Reuel’s daughter, who became the wife of Moses (Ex. 2:21). In consequence of the event recorded in Ex.

3096.d: The Lord protects, a Levite, son of Uzziel (Ex. 6:22).

3101.d: The father of Ephron the Hittite (Gen. 23:8).

3103.d: Snatching (?), one of the sons of Ishi (1 Chr. 4:20).

3104.d: Spreading out, a son of Helem (1 Chr. 7:35), a chief of Asher.

3105.d: Chirping, one of Job’s friends who came to condole with him in his distress (Job 2:11. The LXX. render here “king of the Mineans” = Ma’in, Maonites, Judg. 10:12, in Southern Arabia).

3108.d: Honeycomb, a Kohathite Levite, ancestor of Elkanah and Samuel (1 Sam. 1:1); called also Zophai (1 Chr. 6:26).

3110.d: One of the five Midianite kings whom the Israelites defeated and put to death (Num. 31:8).

3112.d: Rock of God, chief of the family of the Merarites (Num. 3:35) at the time of the Exodus.

3113.d: Rock of the Almighty, the father of Shelumiel, who was chief of the tribe of Simeon when Israel was encamped at Sinai (Num. 1:6; 2:12).

2751.d: A Pharisee in whose house “a woman of the city which was a sinner” anointed our Lord’s feet with ointment (Luke 7:36-38).
